A useful workflow, especially for a first attempt:

  1. **Draft something** : anything, even a bad version. The blank page is the worst page.
  2. **Diagnose** with the 6 Moves. Write a one-sentence verdict for each move: _Move 1 is failed because…_ / _Move 2 is partly done because…_ / _Move 3 is failed because…_ and so on.
  3. **Revise to the worst-failing move first.** Usually this is Move 2 (no specific story) or Move 3 (clichéd opening). Fixing the worst-failing move often pulls the others into shape.
  4. **Re-diagnose.** Go back to step 2 with the revised draft. Repeat until all six moves pass.

A good essay typically goes through three or four iterations of this loop. A great essay goes through six or seven. Most rejected essays go through one — the first draft is submitted with no diagnosis at all.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The 6 Moves
blocks.src:
### 2.10 The Master Pattern: What Readers Want Across All 12 Forms

Before Part II calibrates the 6 Moves to twelve specific forms, it is worth stating the pattern that recurs across all of them. This section is structurally a _preview_ of Part III's synthesis (Chapter 15 returns to these universals with the benefit of having walked through the twelve forms), placed here so the form chapters of Part II can refer back to a shared baseline rather than re-stating universals twelve times. Each form chapter in Part II will return to this pattern with form-specific deviations; the bones below are common to every form.

**What readers want, across the 12 forms:**

  1. **A specific person, not a category.** Whether the reader is Janet on her sofa, Marcus the hiring manager, Professor Lay the graduate-admissions chair, or a USCIS adjudicator, the reader is asking some version of _who is this in particular?_ — and crediting answers that contain enough specifics to pass the Specific Object Test.
  2. **Action over claim.** Specific past actions described in scene support claims about the candidate; abstract claims without action behind them fail across forms.
  3. **Calibrated voice.** The reader wants prose that sounds like a real person — slightly elevated from speech, consistent across the application, not the median register that AI produces by default.
  4. **Genuine fit, not performed adoration.** Whether for a school, a job, a scholarship, or a graduate program, fit is signaled by specific evidence the candidate has done the work to know the institution; flattering generalities are read as performance.
  5. **Honest acknowledgment of limits.** Across forms, the candidate who acknowledges what they have not yet done, what may evolve, and what is uncertain is calibrating their other claims and earning trust. Smoothly polished narratives are vulnerable to contradiction by the rest of the file.

**What readers do not want, across the 12 forms:**

  1. **Inflated language without specifics.** _Passion, dedication, transformative, profound, deep commitment_ — every reader has seen these phrases in a thousand essays. Without specific actions behind them they signal generic candidate.
  2. **Restated information from elsewhere in the file.** The essay is a complement to the resume / transcript / recommendations, not a redundant summary of them.
  3. **Performed humility or performed confidence.** Both register as performance. The reader wants the candidate's actual voice, with calibrated self-assessment.
  4. **The fluent-organized-vague register that AI produces by default.** This is the median register, and the median register is below the bar for any selective context.
  5. **Lessons-learned summaries.** _From this experience, I learned the importance of [virtue]_ in any form is over-explicit and reader-resistant; the Restrained Connection from §2.6 is the calibrated alternative.

**The form-specific calibration is what each chapter in Part II teaches.** A college essay reader has 6–7 minutes; a hiring manager has 30 seconds. A graduate committee reads for research direction; a scholarship committee reads against criteria; an immigration adjudicator reads for verifiable facts. The reader's question changes; the underlying pattern — specifics over abstractions, action over claim, voice over polish, fit over flattery, honesty over performance — does not.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The 6 Moves
blocks.src:
When you read the form chapters, you can read the "What [reader] looks for" / "What [reader] does not look for" sections as the form-specific _deviation_ from this master pattern. The pattern below is your baseline; what the form chapter adds is _how this baseline calibrates to this specific reader, this specific stakes, this specific compression._


### 2.11 Carrying the 6 Moves Into Part II

Each chapter of Part II (Chapters 3 through 14) treats one of the twelve forms of personal persuasion. Each chapter shows the 6 Moves applied to that form's specific demands.

A college essay's Move 1 is Janet on her sofa at 11:23. A cover letter's Move 1 is Marcus the hiring manager between meetings with twelve minutes until standup. A PhD SOP's Move 1 is Professor Lay reading the eighteenth statement of the morning. The reader is different for each form. The first move is to picture the reader concretely.

A college essay's Move 4 might require five Specific Objects in 650 words. A cover letter's Move 4 might require two Specific Objects in 350 words, plus a third that maps onto the role's specific requirements. A PhD SOP's Move 4 might require Specific Objects of a particular kind, methods, papers, data sets, that signal future-colleague.

The 6 Moves are constant. Their calibration to the specific form is what each form chapter teaches.


### 2.12 Reader Draft Prompt

Take the opening line you saved at the end of Chapter 1. Run the 6 Moves on it, in writing.

For each of the six moves, write one to three sentences answering the diagnostic question and giving a specific verdict. Be honest. The point of the exercise is not to feel good about your draft; the point is to know what to fix.

Save your six verdicts. We will return to them in Chapter 3 when the form-specific revision begins.


### 2.13 Exercises

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The 6 Moves
blocks.src:
#### Concept Check

**Q1.** State the 6 Moves and the diagnostic question associated with each.

**Answer:**

  1. Identify the reader and the stakes — _Who is reading this, and what are they actually deciding?_
  2. Find the specific story — _What is the one thing only I can write about this prompt?_
  3. Open with a hook that earns reading — _Why should the reader spend the next 30 seconds with this essay?_
  4. Show with specifics — _Where in this essay are the Specific Objects?_
  5. Connect specifics to claims — _What does this story show, without saying it too directly?_
  6. Survive the AI test — _What in this essay could not have been generated by an AI given my prompt?_

**Q2.** What is the difference between a vignette and an essay?

**Answer:** A vignette is a scene with specifics but no claim about the writer. An essay uses one or more vignettes to support a claim about the writer that the reader, without being told too directly, comes to accept. Move 5 — connect specifics to claims — is the move that turns a vignette into an essay. A vignette without Move 5 is a journal entry; an essay without Moves 4 and 5 is a list.

**Q3.** Why is "I have always been passionate about..." on the _do not_ list for opening lines?

**Answer:** Three reasons. First, the always-having claim is unbelievable: _always_ is the word people use when they cannot remember when they started, which is not the same as always. Second, the construction is the most overused in the genre — every reader has seen it dozens of times this week. Third, the construction commits Move 4 violations: _passionate about_ is abstract, with no Specific Object behind it. The combination of unbelievable, overused, and abstract is fatal.

**Q4.** Describe the Restrained Connection and why it matters.

**Answer:** The Restrained Connection is the move of acknowledging at the end of a vignette that a scene means something without saying everything it means. It is one sentence that lifts the scene's gravity onto the page without pinning it down. It matters because over-connection ("from this experience, I learned the importance of resilience") makes the reader recoil, while under-connection (no claim at all) leaves the reader inventing claims the writer did not intend. The Restrained Connection is the calibrated middle.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The 6 Moves
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1. Diagnose with the 6 Moves.**

Below is the opening of a college essay. Run all 6 Moves on it. Write one to two sentences per move stating which part is done well and which is failed.

> Throughout my life, I have always been deeply passionate about the field of medicine. Ever since I volunteered at my local hospital during my sophomore year of high school, I have been driven by a desire to help others through scientific innovation. This passion has led me to pursue rigorous coursework in biology, chemistry, and physics, as well as numerous extracurricular activities that have prepared me for a career in healthcare.

Hint

This opening commits multiple violations from the _do not_ list. Each move's diagnosis should be specific.

**Answer:**

* **Move 1:** Failed. The opening is written for the abstract robed body, not for Janet. There is no Reader Visualization; the writer has not pictured a fatigued reader at 11 PM. The register is solemn and bureaucratic, exactly the wrong register for a tired reader scanning for something to keep them awake.
* **Move 2:** Failed. There is no Specific Story. _Volunteering at my local hospital_ is a category, not a scene. The reader does not know what the writer did, or saw, or thought.
* **Move 3:** Catastrophically failed. The opening commits the always-having claim ("I have always been deeply passionate") and the sentimentalized origin story ("Ever since I volunteered..."), both on the explicit _do not_ list. The opening has not earned the next 30 seconds.
* **Move 4:** Failed. The opening contains zero Specific Objects. _Medicine,_ _hospital,_ _biology,_ _chemistry,_ and _physics_ are all categories. The Specific Object Test does not pass.
* **Move 5:** Cannot be performed. There is no scene; there is nothing to connect to a claim. The whole opening is telling without showing.
* **Move 6:** Failed. This opening is exactly what an AI would generate given the prompt "write a college essay about wanting to be a doctor." It would not survive a single iteration of the AI test.

The verdict: this opening fails all six moves. The candidate does not need to _edit_ this paragraph; they need to throw it out and start with Move 2 — find a Specific Story.

**Q2. Rewrite the opening.**

The candidate from Q1 has volunteered at a local hospital, takes biology and chemistry, and wants to study medicine. From those facts, write three different opening sentences (or short two-sentence openings) that pass Moves 2, 3, 4, and 6. You may invent specific scenes consistent with the candidate's profile.

Hint

A Specific Object placed in motion (the first kind of opening that earns reading from §2.4) is a good starting point. Find an object the candidate would plausibly remember.

**Answer:** Three possibilities, each different in approach but each passing the moves:

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The 6 Moves
blocks.src:
1. _The first time I saw a heparin lock, I did not know what it was, and the patient I was assigned to wheel down to imaging, Mr. Akwesi, sixty-eight, three weeks after a stroke, caught me staring at his arm and said, in his careful English, "It's so they don't have to stick me twice." I wheeled him in silence the rest of the way down._ — A Specific Object (the heparin lock), a Specific Person (Mr. Akwesi), and a Specific Action (wheeling in silence) put the opening through Moves 2, 3, 4, and 6.
  2. _In the volunteer office at Mercy Hospital, the second-shift coordinator kept a list on her desk of patients without family — column one was room number, column two was first name only, column three was the time she had last seen them awake. I copied the list every Saturday for two years._ — A Specific Object (the list with three columns), a specific habitual action (copying it every Saturday for two years), and an implication left for the reader to draw out.
  3. _My biology teacher told me the right way to look at a slide is the way she taught us in tenth grade: focus first with the lowest-power objective, then increase magnification, never the other way. I have thought about that order more than once, and not only when looking at slides._ — A Specific Object (the slide and the lowest-power objective), a specific person (the biology teacher), and a Restrained Connection at the end.

Each opening earns the next 30 seconds. Each places at least two Specific Objects in motion. None could be plausibly generated by an AI given the bare prompt.

**Q3. The Restrained Connection.**

Below is a vignette without Move 5 — that is, a vignette that has not yet connected to a claim. Write three different one-sentence Restrained Connections that could end this vignette, each connecting to a slightly different implied claim.

> The night the dryer broke, my mother and I hung the laundry on a line strung from the back fence to the apricot tree. She did the shirts; I did the towels. She did not speak for the first ten minutes, and then she said, We've done worse. I held a pillowcase in front of me and looked at it for a long time before I clipped it.

Hint

A Restrained Connection lifts the gravity without pinning it down. It often refers obliquely to the scene's specifics.

**Answer:**

  1. _I have thought about the phrase We've done worse more often since._
  2. _The pillowcase has hung on every clothesline in our house since._
  3. _That was the first time I understood that some things my mother said were also instructions._

Each Restrained Connection connects to a different implied claim:

  1. The phrase becomes a touchstone for the writer about resilience, without using the word.
  2. The pillowcase becomes a recurring object — a Specific Object that travels through the writer's life.
  3. The mother's speech becomes coded instruction, and the writer learned to listen for it.

Each could lead the essay in a different direction. None of them say _I learned about resilience._ The reader does the inferring, which is exactly what Move 5 calls for.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The 6 Moves
blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Move 6 — survive the AI test — is the newest move in this book, and the one most likely to change as AI models change. Speculate on what Move 6 will look like in 2030, when AI models may be able to generate plausibly idiosyncratic memories on demand. Will the move survive in its current form? If not, what should it become?

**Discussion:** Three positions are defensible. One: even when AI generates plausibly idiosyncratic memories, the reader's response will diverge from their response to genuine specificity once they know AI is the source. The move survives, possibly renamed (a _Verifiable Specificity_ test, where readers probe the writer about details). Two: AI-generated specificity becomes indistinguishable at the level of prose, and readers shift weight to interview performance, recommender corroboration, real-time tasks. The move dies and is replaced. Three: the genre shifts away from long-form essays toward forms AI cannot easily fake, and Move 6 evolves to track the new specificity. The book's best guess: Move 6 survives in some form for the next five to ten years, then evolves or is replaced. The other five Moves are more durable.

**Q2.** The 6 Moves are presented as universal across the twelve forms. Is there a thirteenth form, a kind of personal persuasive writing not covered in this book, for which one of the moves does not apply? Sketch the form and the move.

**Discussion:** Two candidates are useful. Consider _the obituary the writer pre-writes for a public figure they admire_ — a kind of indirect personal persuasion. Move 1 (identify the reader and stakes) gets harder because the reader is diffuse; Move 6 (survive the AI test) matters more than ever, since AI generates generic eulogies easily. Or consider _the donation appeal letter from a nonprofit's founder._ Move 2 (find the specific story) is form-defining; Move 5 (connect specifics to claims) becomes the entire letter; Move 1 has a specific reader profile (donors, often older, often skimming). The deeper observation: the 6 Moves are universal across most personal persuasive writing, though calibrations vary. Mastering them on the twelve forms in Part II equips the reader to adapt to any thirteenth form they meet.

**Q3.** Pick a piece of advice you have received about writing personal essays, from a parent, a teacher, a counselor, a book, and run it through the 6 Moves. Does the advice align with one of the moves? Is it actionable? Where does the advice come up short?

**Discussion:** Answers will vary widely. Some common cases: _Tell your story_ aligns with Move 2 but is too vague to be actionable without further specification. _Hook the reader_ aligns with Move 3 but does not say how to hook. _Be authentic_ maps awkwardly onto Move 6 but uses a word ("authentic") that is so saturated with generic use that it has lost meaning. The exercise is meant to show that the 6 Moves are a more operational language than most popular advice — and that a reader who has internalized the Moves can translate any new advice into actionable terms by mapping it onto the Moves.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The 6 Moves
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

The 6 Moves of personal persuasion are the operational vocabulary for the rest of this book. Identify the reader and the stakes; find the specific story; open with a hook that earns reading; show with specifics; connect specifics to claims; survive the AI test.

Each of the form chapters in Part II (Chapters 3 through 14) returns to these six. Chapter 3 calibrates them for the college personal essay (where Janet on her sofa at 11:23 is the reader). Chapter 8 calibrates them for the cover letter (where Marcus the hiring manager between meetings is the reader). Chapter 14 returns most directly to Move 6 — survive the AI test — and lays out the brainstorm-edit-only AI workflow that makes Move 6 reliably passable.

The reader who has done the Reader Draft Prompt, running the 6 Moves on the opening line saved in Chapter 1, has the diagnostic in hand. The next chapter begins the calibration. Whether the diagnostic produces a better essay depends on what the reader does with it. The book teaches the discipline; the writing is yours.

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
Top-school admissions readers spend, by the rough estimate that has circulated among admissions officers for two decades, six to seven minutes on each application essay during peak season. Some Ivy League readers process fifty essays per day. The first thirty seconds determine whether they read it carefully.

This chapter is about the essay that has more attention paid to it than any other in the personal-persuasion universe and gets read for less time than its writers imagine. The Common App personal essay is 650 words long. The reader will spend, at most, six minutes on it. The goal of every craft decision in this chapter is to make those six minutes useful.


### 3.1 Vignette: Theo's First Draft

Theo, our continuing applicant, sits down on a Saturday morning in late September of senior year to write the Common App personal essay. The Common App prompt Theo has chosen is the open-ended one: _Some students have a background, identity, interest, or talent that is so meaningful they believe their application would be incomplete without it. If this sounds like you, please share your story._

Theo writes the following first draft.

> I have always been passionate about helping people. Ever since I was a little girl, I knew I wanted to make a difference in the world. Whether it was tutoring younger students at the local community center, organizing the school's annual food drive, or mentoring incoming freshmen on the soccer team, I have consistently sought out opportunities to give back to my community.
> 
> One of the most formative experiences of my life was tutoring at the Eastview Community Center. Every Saturday morning for two years, I worked with elementary school students who were struggling with reading. I learned the importance of patience, perseverance, and the power of one-on-one connection. Many of these students came from immigrant families, and I found myself drawing on my own background as the granddaughter of a Salvadoran immigrant.
> 
> My grandmother came to the United States in 1983 with very little. Her resilience and dedication to providing a better life for her family inspired me deeply. She taught me the value of hard work, the importance of family, and the power of perseverance in the face of adversity. These lessons have shaped who I am today and will continue to guide me as I pursue my goals in college and beyond.
> 
> [The draft continues for another 380 words in the same register.]

Theo reads the draft. Theo's instinct says it is fine. Theo's instinct is wrong, and the rest of this chapter explains why.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
### 3.2 What Admissions Readers Actually Do

Janet, the reader from Chapter 1, opens Theo's essay at 9:14 PM on a Tuesday. She has read twenty-two essays so far this evening. She has eighteen more in tonight's queue. Her process, repeated thousands of times across her career:

  1. **Read the first two sentences carefully** (about 10 seconds).
  2. **Decide whether to read carefully** or skim. The decision is mostly automatic at this point in her career; she has read enough essays to recognize the patterns within seconds.
  3. **If skimming** : read the first sentence of each paragraph, glance at the closing paragraph, type a one-word note.
  4. **If reading carefully** : read the whole essay, often pausing to read sentences twice, and write a longer note.

Janet's queue tonight contains forty essays. Of those, she will read perhaps eight carefully — the ones that survived the first thirty seconds. The other thirty-two she will skim and dismiss with a one-word note.

The math is brutal: only twenty percent of essays get the careful read the candidate hoped for. Theo's first draft will not be in the twenty percent.


#### What Janet Looks For (And What She Does Not)

Janet does not look for a candidate who claims passion. The application has thirteen other places where the candidate's commitments can be inferred (extracurricular list, awards, recommendation letters, course selection). The essay is not the place to _claim_ commitment; the essay is the place to _show_ a candidate as a specific human.

Beyond the universal pattern in §2.10, Janet specifically weighs:

  1. **A small action that reveals a large pattern.** Janet reads without a rubric, inferring _who is this_ from one specific moment that lets her predict the candidate's unscripted Tuesdays.
  2. **A surprise.** Janet reads ninety essays a day. Something she did not expect earns the next thirty seconds — and signals the candidate has not constructed the essay by guessing at what Janet wants.
  3. **Voice she'd want to read for four years.** Janet is admitting this candidate to a community of writers and thinkers. She is asking, on the side of her attention, _would I want to read this person's writing for the next four years?_

Janet does not look for, beyond the universals:

  1. The candidate's narration of the candidate's own emotional growth.
  2. Performances of gratitude or perspective in the register of a college admissions essay as imagined by someone who has read about them but has not read many.


### 3.3 Genre Conventions

The Common App personal essay has accreted conventions over the past two decades. Knowing the conventions does not mean obeying all of them; it means knowing which to obey, which to push against, and which are dead.


#### The Length Convention

650 words is the upper bound, not a target. Going under signals nothing wrong (a dense 480-word essay can beat a padded 650); going over is impossible (the Common App truncates). See §15.4.1 for the consolidated cross-form reference.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
#### The Opening Convention

The first sentence should give Janet a reason to read on. The conventions here are stable:

* **Specific Object placed in motion** is the strongest opening. The opening of Theo's revised essay (the green plastic radio) is in this mode.
* **Surprising claim that the essay will defend** is a close second. _I am a worse student than my GPA suggests, and the reasons matter_ is a strong opening because it earns the read by promising a specific defense.
* **Scene with a small action** is the third strong mode. _When my mother lost her job, I figured out how to apply for SNAP for our family — and then I started helping the other ESL families at our church figure it out too_ is in this mode.

The opening conventions to avoid are on the _do not_ list from Chapter 2: famous quotes, thesis statements, dictionary definitions, slow scene-setting, always-having claims, sentimentalized origin stories.


#### The Specific Story Convention

A successful Common App essay typically tells _one_ story in detail rather than three stories in summary. The 650-word constraint does not allow three stories to be told well. The candidate who tries to cram in the soccer captaincy, the tutoring program, and the grandmother's immigration in 650 words ends up with three thin stories and no specific person on the page.

Pick one. Develop it. The other two might appear briefly as supporting details, but only one is the spine.


#### The Reflection Convention

A successful Common App essay reflects on the story it tells, but the reflection is restrained. The Restrained Connection from Chapter 2 (Move 5) is the operational tool. The reflection should land in one or two sentences, late in the essay, and should not pin the meaning down so hard that the reader resists.

The dead version of this convention: closing the essay with _and from this experience, I learned the importance of..._ This phrase is on the implicit _do not_ list of every admissions reader.


#### The Voice Convention

A successful Common App essay sounds like a specific seventeen- or eighteen-year-old, not like a college admissions consultant. The voice should be conversational, knowledgeable but not pretentious, occasionally funny, occasionally serious. It should sound like a smart kid who happens to be writing in formal sentences, not like a professional writer trying to perform youth.

The voice convention is hard to teach directly. The most useful test: read the essay aloud to a friend who knows you. If the friend says _that doesn't sound like you,_ you have written in the wrong voice. Revise toward your actual speech, with one degree of polish added.


#### The Length-Per-Paragraph Convention

Long paragraphs are hard to scan. The Common App essay benefits from three- to six-sentence paragraphs that each do one thing. A wall-of-text paragraph that runs twelve sentences is a paragraph the skimming reader will not enter. A reader's eye lands on the first sentence of each paragraph; that sentence has to do work.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
### 3.4 Theo's First Draft Run Through the 6 Moves

Recall Theo's first draft from §3.1. Let us run the 6 Moves on it in detail.

**Move 1 (Identify the reader):** Failed. Theo wrote for the abstract robed body. The opening line is in the always-having register. Janet, on her sofa at 9:14, scans the first two sentences and decides to skim.

**Move 2 (Find the specific story):** Failed. Theo's draft tries to cover three stories (tutoring, food drive, mentoring) in 650 words. None of them gets developed. The grandmother's immigration is mentioned but not seen.

**Move 3 (Open with a hook):** Catastrophically failed. _I have always been passionate_ and _Ever since I was a little girl_ are both on the explicit _do not_ list.

**Move 4 (Show with specifics):** Failed. The draft contains zero Specific Objects in the first two paragraphs. _Eastview Community Center_ is named but not seen — no description, no scene, no object. The grandmother is named but not seen.

**Move 5 (Connect specifics to claims):** Done badly. Each paragraph closes with a generic claim ("I learned the importance of patience, perseverance, and the power of one-on-one connection"). The connection is over-explicit and over-generic.

**Move 6 (Survive the AI test):** Failed. The draft is exactly what an AI would generate given the prompt "write a college essay about wanting to help people." The whole essay could be auto-completed by a 2023-era model.

The verdict: Theo's draft fails all six moves. The remedy is not to edit; it is to start over from Move 2.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
#### Theo's Second Draft

Theo applies the diagnostic from Chapter 2. Theo searches memory for a Specific Object. Theo lands, again, on the green plastic radio. The radio becomes the spine of a different essay.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
> My grandmother kept the green plastic radio in her kitchen tuned to the AM Spanish-language station even after she stopped speaking Spanish at home. I asked her once why. She said, _You don't need to understand to listen._
> 
> She had stopped speaking Spanish at home in 1991, the year my mother turned twelve and asked her to. My mother had not wanted the kids at school to know. My grandmother had agreed, on the condition that the radio would stay on. _Quiet,_ she had said. _But on._ In 1991 she was thirty-eight years old and had lived in this country for eight years.
> 
> I learned about this transaction the way I learned about most things in our family: in fragments, not on purpose. My mother told me one piece while we were folding laundry. My grandmother told me another piece while she was cutting peppers. No one ever sat me down to explain.
> 
> The radio still sat on the kitchen counter when I was seventeen. The dial was set to 1480 AM, the same station my grandmother had set it to in 1991. The station played mariachi most of the day, news at the top of the hour in Spanish, and a call-in show on Saturday afternoons that I had only ever heard from across the room. I had taken Spanish for three years in high school. I could understand the news at the top of the hour, mostly. I could not understand the call-in show.
> 
> The summer before senior year, I started turning the radio louder. Not when my grandmother was in the room, she would have known what I was doing and resented it, but when I was alone in the kitchen making lunch, or when I came home before her from the tutoring center where I worked on Saturdays. I wanted to understand. I had decided, without telling anyone, that I would speak Spanish with my grandmother before I left for college.
> 
> I will not tell you that this worked. The summer was hard. My Spanish was textbook Spanish; the radio was Salvadoran Spanish, which is different in ways my high school teacher had not prepared me for. The call-in show used words I did not know and idioms I could not parse. I would catch a phrase, then lose it, then catch another. By August I had not yet had the conversation with my grandmother I had wanted to have.
> 
> What I had instead was a habit of listening to a language I was not yet fluent in. I learned, slowly, to sit in not-understanding without panicking. I learned that comprehension is not binary; it is a curve, and you can be useful on the curve before you arrive at fluency. I learned this from the radio and from one specific evening in late July, when the call-in show host opened with a sentence about the upcoming election in El Salvador that I did not understand, and I let myself not understand, and listened anyway.
> 
> Three weeks later my grandmother and I were chopping peppers together. The radio was on. I asked her, in Spanish, what the host had been talking about. My grandmother did not look up from the peppers. She said, in English, _He always talks about the election. He has been talking about the election since I came here._ Then she said, in Spanish, _You are listening._
> 
> I did not have the conversation with her in Spanish that I had been planning. I had the conversation in two languages, switching whichever way the topic asked. _You don't need to understand to listen,_ she had said years before. By the end of that summer I had begun to suspect what she actually meant.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
This second draft is approximately 600 words. It contains specific objects (the green plastic radio, the dial set to 1480 AM, the call-in show, the peppers); a specific story (the summer of trying to learn Spanish via the radio); a hook that earns reading; and a Restrained Connection at the end (_By the end of that summer I had begun to suspect what she actually meant_) that lifts the gravity without pinning it down.

Run the 6 Moves on the second draft:

* **Move 1** : Done. Janet on her sofa is engaged within the first two sentences.
* **Move 2** : Done. One Specific Story (the summer with the radio).
* **Move 3** : Done. The opening Specific Object earns the read.
* **Move 4** : Done. The Specific Object Test passes — at least three concrete objects (radio, dial, peppers).
* **Move 5** : Done with restraint. The closing sentence connects without pinning down.
* **Move 6** : Done. No AI given a generic prompt would have produced this essay. The grandmother's exact 1991 transaction with the mother, the dial set to 1480, the late-July evening, the bilingual exchange over peppers — these are Theo's, not generic.

The second draft is not perfect. It will go through three more revisions — tightening sentences, adjusting paragraph breaks, removing one paragraph that turns out to be redundant on second reading. But the spine of the essay is now in place.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
### 3.5 A Complete Sample Essay

Below is a complete original college essay written by a fictional applicant, Mei. Mei is a high school senior in Sacramento, California, the daughter of Vietnamese immigrants. The Common App prompt: _Reflect on a time when you questioned or challenged a belief or idea._

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
> When I was fourteen, my father asked me to help him at the cash register of his pho restaurant on a Tuesday afternoon, and I learned that I had been wrong about a regular customer named Mr. Davis.
> 
> Mr. Davis had eaten lunch at our restaurant four days a week for as long as I could remember. He always ordered the same thing: small beef pho, no onions, extra lime. He paid in cash. He sat at the same table by the window. He was, as far as I knew, a quiet man in late middle age who liked our pho and did not like to chat. I had served him hundreds of times. I had not exchanged twenty words with him over a decade.
> 
> The Tuesday I worked the register, Mr. Davis came in at his usual time, ordered his usual order, paid his usual five dollars in singles, and then said to me, _Tell your father the new sriracha is too sweet._
> 
> I had not known he had opinions about the sriracha. I had not known he had opinions about anything. I told my father.
> 
> My father said, _Of course it is too sweet. He is right._ Then my father told me, in Vietnamese while we were closing, that Mr. Davis had eaten at our restaurant since the second month it was open. He had been a regular for nineteen years. He had never once not paid. He had once, during the 2012 wildfires, brought my father a case of bottled water without explanation. My father had returned the case. Mr. Davis had brought a different case the next day, and my father had given up.
> 
> I asked my father what Mr. Davis did. My father did not know. I asked my father if he had ever been to Mr. Davis's house. My father had not. I asked my father what they talked about. My father said, _The pho. The weather. His knee. My back._
> 
> The next Tuesday I served Mr. Davis. I asked him, while pouring his iced tea, how his knee was. Mr. Davis looked at me as if I had crossed a small line. Then he said, _Bad. The new doctor is worse than the old one._ I asked him about the old doctor. He told me. The conversation lasted perhaps four minutes. Mr. Davis paid and left.
> 
> I had been wrong about Mr. Davis. I had assumed, for ten years of serving him pho, that his quietness meant he had no relationship with us. The opposite was true. His quietness was the relationship. He had been our most loyal customer in a way I had not been able to read because I was looking for the wrong signals.
> 
> Vietnamese has an idea, _tình nghĩa_ , that does not translate cleanly to English. It is something between loyalty, gratitude, and a quiet long-term obligation that does not require expression. My grandmother, who taught me the word, used it most often about people who had done something kind a long time ago and were owed a corresponding kindness for the rest of one's life.
> 
> Mr. Davis had been practicing _tình nghĩa_ in our restaurant for nineteen years without anyone in my family naming it. My father had been receiving it in the same register without ever asking who Mr. Davis was outside the restaurant. The transaction did not need expression. The expression I would have wanted — chatting, asking after his weekend, treating him like an old friend — would have ruined what was actually there.
> 
> I have thought about Mr. Davis often since. I am about to leave for college, where I will meet hundreds of people whose quietness I might mistake for absence. I think I will be slower to read people from the surface than I used to be. I think I will sit longer in not-understanding. The word _tình nghĩa_ has a stricter rule for me now than I had ten years ago: it is something you owe to people you do not yet know that you owe.
> 
> Mr. Davis still comes to the restaurant on Tuesdays. He still orders small beef pho, no onions, extra lime. We have, over the past three years, learned to talk about his knee, the weather, my college applications, his old doctor, my brother's basketball team. He has not mentioned the sriracha again. We have not changed it back.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
Notes on what this essay is doing:

* **Move 1** : written for Janet on her sofa. The first sentence places Janet inside a specific scene with a question. Janet reads on.
* **Move 2** : one Specific Story (the Tuesday afternoon at the cash register, expanded into a longer arc with Mr. Davis). Not three stories crammed into one essay.
* **Move 3** : the opening sentence gives the reader a specific scene with a small surprise (_I had been wrong about a regular customer named Mr. Davis_). The reader wants to find out how.
* **Move 4** : many Specific Objects — the small beef pho, no onions, extra lime, the cash register, the iced tea, the case of bottled water, the 2012 wildfires.
* **Move 5** : connections are mostly restrained. _I had been wrong about Mr. Davis_ is connection. _I have thought about Mr. Davis often since_ is connection. The Vietnamese word _tình nghĩa_ is connection that does its work without overstatement.
* **Move 6** : the AI test passes. The exact characters of Mr. Davis, the case of bottled water during the 2012 wildfires, the four-minute conversation about the old doctor, the bilingual closing — these are not generic; an AI given a bare prompt would not produce this combination.

This essay is not exceptional in any obvious way. The candidate is not a recruited athlete or a national award winner. The story is a small story about a small relationship. _And yet:_ Janet, on her sofa at 9:14 PM, will remember this candidate two weeks later. She will remember Mei as _the kid with Mr. Davis and the sriracha._ That is enough. That is the goal of this form.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
#### A Second Sample: Different Background, Same Discipline

Mei's essay draws on cultural heritage, language, and family. A note about whether you need that kind of material: **you don't.** The Specific Object Test does not require an immigrant grandmother or a heritage-language home. It requires a specific life, lived attentively. Below is a second complete sample that demonstrates the principles using a candidate with no immigrant-family material — the kind of candidate whose personal-essay anxiety often runs _I don't have anything interesting to write about._

The candidate is Ben, a high school senior in Marshalltown, Iowa (population 27,000). His father runs a feed store; his mother is a school nurse. He has been a serious bird-watcher since age nine. Common App prompt: _Some students have a background, identity, interest, or talent that is so meaningful they believe their application would be incomplete without it._

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
> The sandhill cranes come through Marshall County in mid-October. There are a hundred and twenty thousand of them, give or take, and they stop on the same set of cornfields every year before continuing south. I learned this in fifth grade from a man named Roger Linnenbrink, who is sixty-eight, retired from Iowa State, and parks his Subaru on the gravel turnout north of County Road E63 every fall morning between October 12 and November 4. I started parking next to him when I was thirteen.
> 
> Roger keeps two notebooks in his glove compartment. One is for the cranes — count, time, weather, wind direction. The other is for everyone who pulls over to ask him what he is looking at. By the time I was fifteen I had read both. I asked him once why he kept the second notebook. He said, _Because most of them never come back._
> 
> Roger has been counting cranes in the same fields for thirty-one years. The count he recorded the morning I first met him was 14,847 birds. The count he recorded last October 19, the morning I told him I had been admitted to Iowa State through rolling admission, was 9,213. The thirty-one-year average is somewhere around 12,000. Roger does not extrapolate. He keeps the numbers and lets the numbers speak.
> 
> The first morning I tried to count without Roger, I was sixteen and the fog had come in over the corn before dawn. Roger had been at a funeral in Des Moines. I drove out with his old binoculars and a thermos. I counted 3,140 birds in the south field by 8:15. When the fog lifted at 9:40 I counted again and got 4,520. I had been double-counting groups as they rose and resettled in the fog. My notebook entry that morning reads, in pencil: _3,140 fog count, 4,520 clear count, see Roger. Probably 4,520. Probably not._ I drove out to his house that evening and showed him the page. He read it twice and said, _Write down what you saw and the conditions you saw it in. The numbers fix themselves over a few seasons._ That sentence is the first entry I made, when I got home, in the second notebook — not the bird notebook — about a person.
> 
> What I learned from Roger is not what I expected to learn. I expected to learn about birds. I did learn about birds — that sandhills mate for life and remember field locations across generations, that the average bird in the flock is older than I am, that the migration route shifted west by about thirty miles in the 1990s for reasons that are still debated. But the deeper lesson was about the second notebook. Most of the people Roger met in those thirty-one years asked him what he was looking at, listened to his answer for ninety seconds, and drove on. The few who came back came back many times. _The cranes are the test_ , Roger told me once. _The people who come back are the ones who do not need the cranes to be more than they are._
> 
> I have kept my own notebook since I was fifteen. It is mostly the cranes — same fields, same dates. But there are also entries for the people who pulled over: Mr. Hesseltine, a retired pilot who knew the cranes' migration patterns from above and who taught me the word _thermals;_ a woman from Cedar Rapids who came every year to scatter her sister's ashes in the same field and who never asked the bird questions, only sat in her car; the high school biology teacher who started bringing her freshmen on a field trip the year I was a sophomore. These notebook entries, more than my AP Biology grades, are why I want to study ornithology and conservation. The cranes will be there or they will not be there. The notebook is the thing I can keep.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
Notes on what this essay does:

* **Move 1** : Janet on her sofa at 9:30 PM. The opening sentence places her in a specific Iowa cornfield with a specific number (a hundred and twenty thousand birds). She reads on.
* **Move 2** : One Specific Story (the relationship with Roger across thirty-one years of crane counts).
* **Move 3** : The opening — a precise number of cranes, a specific man, a specific gravel turnout — promises specificity. The reader stays.
* **Move 4** : Many Specific Objects: the gravel turnout north of County Road E63, the dates October 12–November 4, the two notebooks, the count 14,847 / 9,213 / thirty-one-year average around 12,000, the fog-morning miscount (3,140 / 4,520), Roger's sentence about the conditions, Mr. Hesseltine the retired pilot, the woman from Cedar Rapids, the high school biology teacher.
* **Move 5** : Restrained Connection at the close: _the notebook is the thing I can keep_ signals the meaning of the relationship without spelling out the lesson. The earlier _the cranes are the test_ line — Roger's, not Ben's — does similar work earlier in the essay.
* **Move 6** : The AI test passes. The specific gravel turnout, the specific count numbers, Roger Linnenbrink's name and age, the second notebook, the woman scattering her sister's ashes — none of these are generic. An AI given the prompt _write a college essay about being a bird-watcher in rural Iowa_ would not produce this combination.

What Mei's essay and Ben's essay have in common is not background. It is _attention._ Both candidates noticed something specific, kept noticing it across years, and have a specific small thing to write about. Mei has Mr. Davis; Ben has Roger and the cranes. The difference between this kind of essay and the generic kind is not what the candidate has — it is what the candidate has paid attention to. The Specific Object Inventory from §2.3.3 is the practice that surfaces material like this.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
### 3.6 Common Pitfalls

Five pitfalls account for most of the essays Janet skims and dismisses.

**Pitfall 1: The trauma-to-triumph template.** A candidate has experienced something hard (a parent's illness, a family financial setback, a sports injury). The candidate writes the essay in the template _I had a hard thing; I overcame it; here is what I learned._ The template is overused enough that Janet recognizes it within the opening paragraph. Her response is not to be moved; her response is to mark the candidate as a writer who has used a template.

The remedy: tell the same story without the template. Skip the _here is what I learned_ close. Let the reader infer. Spend more words on the specific scenes within the hard thing rather than on the hard thing's emotional summary. The hard thing matters less than the specific Tuesday inside the hard thing.

**Pitfall 2: The genericized identity essay.** A candidate writes about their identity (immigrant, first-generation, queer, Black, Asian, low-income, religious) in language so generic that the essay could be written by any candidate with that identity. The reader, who has read forty essays this week with similar identities, cannot distinguish the candidate from the others.

The remedy: do not write about your identity in the abstract. Write about a specific moment, with specific objects, in which your identity was operating in the background. The reader will infer the identity. The essay will become specifically yours.

**Pitfall 3: The retrospective self-congratulation.** A candidate writes about a project they led, an award they won, an obstacle they overcame, in a register that subtly congratulates the candidate for having done the thing. _Through hard work and dedication, I was able to lead my team to a regional championship._ The reader, who has read this register hundreds of times, hears the self-congratulation immediately and discounts it.

The remedy: tell the story in present tense, in scene, without the retrospective wrap-up. Let the reader notice the leadership rather than have it asserted. _In the second half against Westview, when my keeper twisted her ankle and waved me back, I had nine seconds to call the substitution before the throw-in_ is showing leadership. _I demonstrated leadership through challenge_ is asserting it.

**Pitfall 4: The dead-pet essay.** Many candidates have lost a beloved pet and feel the pet was an important figure in their lives. The pet essay is overrepresented in admissions queues. Janet has read the pet essay thirty times this season. The pet essay can be written well, but the writer faces an uphill climb against reader fatigue with the form.

The remedy, if you must write about the pet: write about a specific concrete moment with the pet, not about the pet as a category. Skip the death of the pet entirely (Janet is exhausted by pet deaths). Focus on an unexpected day, an unusual habit of the pet, a small action you took for or with the pet. The pet is allowed; the pet-as-grief-vessel is overdone.

**Pitfall 5: The voice mismatch.** A candidate adopts a voice that does not sound like them — most often, a more "literary" or "mature" or "sophisticated" voice that the candidate has been told sounds appropriate for college admissions. The voice mismatch is detectable. Janet hears the candidate trying on a costume.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
The remedy: read your essay aloud. If a sentence does not sound like you, rewrite it in your actual voice with one degree of polish. Voice should be slightly elevated from speech, not transformed.


### 3.7 Cultural and ESL Calibration

Many readers of this book are ESL applicants writing for U.S. admissions. The conventions of the U.S. admissions essay are culturally specific in ways that can disadvantage applicants from other writing traditions.

The U.S. admissions essay favors:

* Showing personal vulnerability and emotion, in moderation.
* Specific small moments rather than grand abstractions.
* A first-person voice that is conversational, not formal.
* A claim about the writer that the reader infers from a story rather than is told directly.

Many other writing traditions favor:

* Formal academic register, even in personal contexts.
* General principles supported by examples, rather than specific stories that imply principles.
* Modesty about personal vulnerability.
* Direct claims about the writer's qualities.

ESL writers educated in some traditions arrive at the U.S. admissions essay defaulting to the second column. Their essays are formal, modest, principled — and underperform with U.S. readers, who do not recognize the merits of the form.

The remedy is not to abandon one's own writing tradition. The remedy is to recognize that the U.S. admissions essay is _its own genre_ with conventions that can be learned. A writer can master the conventions without abandoning their broader literary identity. The conventions are tools; they are not values.

For the ESL writer, the Specific Object Test is especially useful. It cuts through the formal-register default. It forces the essay onto particular Tuesday afternoons, particular cash registers, particular pho with no onions and extra lime. The Specific Object Test is culturally portable in a way that "be yourself" is not.


### 3.8 Reader Draft Prompt

Take the opening line you saved at the end of Chapter 1 and the 6 Moves verdict you wrote at the end of Chapter 2.

Now write a new opening, three to five sentences, that performs Move 3 (open with a hook that earns reading) using a Specific Object placed in motion. The Specific Object should be drawn from your own life. It should not be the most impressive thing you have done. It should be small, particular, and remembered.

Compare the new opening to the old. Save both. We will return to them in Chapter 17.


### 3.9 Exercises

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
#### Concept Check

**Q1.** State the average reading time per essay for selective-school admissions readers during peak season.

**Answer:** Six to seven minutes. Some readers spend more (faculty on final committees: 10–20 minutes). Some spend less (first-pass readers at high-volume institutions: 3 minutes). The average across selective institutions and reading rounds is in the six-to-seven range.

**Q2.** Why is the trauma-to-triumph template overused, and what is the remedy?

**Answer:** The template is overused because many candidates have experienced something hard and assume the proper essay structure is _hard thing → overcoming → lesson learned._ Janet has seen the template enough to recognize it within the opening paragraph. The remedy is to tell the same story without the template — skip the lesson-learned close, let the reader infer, spend more words on specific scenes within the hard thing rather than on the hard thing's emotional summary.

**Q3.** What does the Specific Object Test require for a college personal essay?

**Answer:** At least three Specific Objects — particular times, places, actions, or objects that only the writer could have written. A 650-word essay typically benefits from four to six Specific Objects distributed throughout, not concentrated in the opening paragraph.

**Q4.** What is the difference between _showing_ leadership and _asserting_ leadership in a college essay?

**Answer:** Showing leadership puts the reader inside a scene where the candidate is making a leadership decision in specific circumstances ("In the second half against Westview, when my keeper twisted her ankle and waved me back, I had nine seconds to call the substitution before the throw-in"). Asserting leadership uses general claims about the candidate's leadership qualities ("I demonstrated leadership through challenge"). Showing is durable and memorable; asserting is generic and easily skimmed.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1. Diagnose this opening.**

> Throughout my journey as a high school student, I have had the privilege of pursuing a wide variety of activities, ranging from competitive debate to community service to my role as captain of the varsity tennis team. Each of these experiences has shaped me into the person I am today.

Run the 6 Moves on this opening. Identify which moves are failed and explain in one sentence each why.

Hint

The opening commits at least four of the six moves badly. Be specific.

**Answer:**

* Move 1: Failed. The opening is written for the abstract robed body, not for Janet. The register is bureaucratic ("had the privilege of pursuing").
* Move 2: Failed. No Specific Story. Three categories (debate, community service, tennis) listed without any scene.
* Move 3: Failed. The opening does not earn the read. _Throughout my journey_ is on the implicit _do not_ list. _Each of these experiences has shaped me_ is empty.
* Move 4: Failed. Zero Specific Objects.
* Move 5: Cannot be performed; there is no specific to connect to a claim.
* Move 6: Failed. The opening is exactly what an AI would generate.

The remedy is to discard this opening entirely and start with Move 2 — find a Specific Story.

**Q2. Rewrite an opening.**

A candidate has been the captain of the varsity tennis team for two years. From this fact alone, write three different opening sentences (or two-sentence openings) that pass Moves 2, 3, 4, and 6. You may invent specific scenes consistent with the candidate's profile.

Hint

The Specific Object Test should pass within the opening. The opening should not say _captain_ or _leadership_ or _team._

**Answer:** Three possibilities:

  1. _In the second half of the regional final against Lincoln, when my doubles partner Yuki served the third double-fault in a row, I called a timeout and asked her what she had eaten for breakfast. The answer turned out to matter._
  2. _The first time I held the team meeting after Coach Reyes left for paternity leave, I had not yet figured out what to call myself when I addressed the team. I tried "Captain Choi" once, in private, in the locker room mirror, and never said it again._
  3. _We kept a notebook in the tennis storage closet, bequeathed by the previous captain to the next, refusing the digital era, in which each captain wrote one true sentence about each year before handing it off. My sentence took me three months to write._

Each opening passes the Specific Object Test (specific objects: the third double-fault, Lincoln, breakfast / the locker room mirror, "Captain Choi" / the notebook in the storage closet, the previous captain). None says _leadership._ All three earn the next thirty seconds.

**Q3. Diagnose a sample essay's pitfalls.**

Below is the closing paragraph of a candidate's college essay about volunteering at a homeless shelter:

> Through my time at the Hope Mission Shelter, I learned the importance of empathy, the value of service, and the power of community. These lessons have shaped who I am today and will continue to guide me as I pursue my future endeavors. I am incredibly grateful for the opportunity to have made a difference in the lives of so many.

Identify the pitfalls and rewrite the paragraph using the Restrained Connection from Chapter 2.

Hint

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
The current paragraph commits the lessons-learned summary, the retrospective self-congratulation, and the genericized identity. The remedy is to land one specific sentence that does Move 5 with restraint.

**Answer:** The current paragraph commits three pitfalls — lessons-learned summary ("I learned the importance of empathy, the value of service, and the power of community"), retrospective self-congratulation ("the opportunity to have made a difference in the lives of so many"), and the genericized identity essay (the candidate becomes interchangeable with every other shelter-volunteer candidate). A Restrained Connection version:

> The list on the bulletin board still has fifteen names on it. I check it before I leave each Wednesday, the way you check a tide chart before walking out onto a flat. I do not yet know what I will do with the names after I leave for college. I know I will check the list again at Thanksgiving.

The Restrained Connection version does Move 5 in concrete terms (the list, the bulletin board, the Wednesday, the Thanksgiving). It does not state what the candidate "learned." It implies a continuing relationship without claiming gratitude. The reader infers the candidate's character from the action of checking the list.

**Q4. Apply the Specific Object Test to your draft.**

Take any 200-word section of an essay you are currently working on (your own draft, or one of the openings you wrote in Q2 above). Highlight every sentence that contains a Specific Object — a particular time, place, action, or object that only you (or someone in your specific life) could have written.

Count the highlights. If fewer than three are highlighted in 200 words, the section fails the Specific Object Test.

Rewrite one un-highlighted sentence so that it now contains a Specific Object.

Hint

You may need to _remember harder_ rather than _write better._ Specificity is a memory exercise, not a vocabulary exercise.

**Answer:** Answers will vary. The exercise's discipline is honest counting. A passing 200-word section has at least three Specific Objects distributed throughout — not all concentrated in one paragraph. If the count is one or two, the rewrite move is to remember a small, specific moment from the larger story being told and place its objects on the page. (Example: a candidate writing about volunteering at the homeless shelter remembers the laminated list of fifteen names on the bulletin board, the specific Wednesday, the specific tide chart metaphor, the specific Thanksgiving check-in. These are Specific Objects that did not appear in the genericized version of the same essay.)

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** The chapter argues that admissions readers are not looking to be flattered, only engaged. Sketch a defense of the _opposite_ claim: that subtle flattery, deployed well, is part of a well-written college essay. Where does the line between _engagement_ and _flattery_ actually fall?

**Discussion:** A subtle defense of the contrarian claim is possible. Engagement requires acknowledging the reader's circumstances, and some acknowledgment shades into flattery. The line falls roughly here: _flattery directed at the institution's prestige_ (X is the country's most selective school) lands on the wrong side; _flattery directed at the reader's intelligence_ — writing as if the reader will catch a subtle joke or a non-obvious connection — often lands on the right side. The book's strong stance is against the first kind, not the second. A candidate who writes a sentence assuming the reader will laugh at a particular small absurdity, and is right, has flattered the reader's perception in a way that engages rather than panders.

**Q2.** The chapter claims that the dead-pet essay is overrepresented in admissions queues and that candidates should approach the form with caution. Yet some essays about pets do get admitted candidates in. What conditions distinguish a successful pet essay from the typical dead-pet essay?

**Discussion:** Three conditions distinguish a successful pet essay. First, the pet is not the subject; the pet is a vehicle for a subject the candidate could not write about directly. (A candidate who learned about her grandfather's dementia by watching him with the family dog has written about dementia, not the dog.) Second, the pet does not die in the essay, or if it does, the death is not the climactic event. Third, the pet has a specific characteristic that defies the genre — a strange habit, an unusual attachment, an unexpected comedic quality. The successful pet essay is about a particular relationship with a particular animal that illuminates the writer; the unsuccessful one is about grief and lesson-learning.

**Q3.** Voice is hard to teach directly. The chapter offers the read-aloud test as a calibration. Propose an alternative test for voice that does not require reading aloud — a test that could be performed at midnight three days before the deadline by a candidate who cannot ask anyone to listen.

**Discussion:** Four alternative tests are useful. First: read each paragraph and ask, _would I send this as a text to my closest friend?_ If no, the paragraph has voice problems. Second: mix three sentences from your essay with three from a recent text message; if a stranger could sort them by tone alone, the essay is too far from your speech. Third: read sentence by sentence backwards — voice problems become more visible once the meaning sequence is broken. Fourth: ask whether each sentence reads in the voice of a 17-year-old or a 45-year-old admissions consultant. The read-aloud test is most efficient, but any of these can substitute when reading aloud is not feasible.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: The College Personal Essay (US Common App)
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

The Common App personal essay is read for six to seven minutes by a tired person at the end of a long day. Every craft decision in this chapter follows from that reality. The 6 Moves from Chapter 2 calibrate to this form by privileging Specific Objects, Specific Stories, and openings that earn the read in the first 30 seconds.

The five common pitfalls — trauma-to-triumph, genericized identity, retrospective self-congratulation, dead-pet, and voice mismatch — account for most of the essays admissions readers skim and dismiss. The Restrained Connection (Move 5) is the move that distinguishes amateur essays from craft essays in this form.

ESL writers educated in different writing traditions arrive at the U.S. admissions essay disadvantaged by their default formal register. The Specific Object Test is culturally portable and especially useful for writers crossing the cultural distance.

The next chapter (Chapter 4) treats the supplements — the _why this school_ and _why this major_ essays that often determine the application. The supplements are shorter, more specific, and require even more genuine school-specific evidence than the personal essay.

The only essay no one else can write is yours. The chapter has shown how to write it. What is left is the writing.

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: College Supplements (Why Us / Why You / Why This Major)
blocks.src:
"Why this school" essays are often the deciding factor between two otherwise comparable applicants. Generic versions effectively reject the candidate.

This is the surprising fact that opens the chapter, and most candidates do not believe it. Most candidates assume the personal essay is the differentiator and the supplements are afterthoughts — short forms to be filled out late at night between chapters of the personal essay. The math at selective institutions says the opposite. When two candidates have indistinguishable transcripts, indistinguishable extracurriculars, and indistinguishable personal essays, the supplements are what decide.

This chapter is about the form of writing that does the deciding.


### 4.1 Vignette: Theo Writes Six Supplements in Three Days

Theo's personal essay is finished. The Common App has been opened. Six schools require additional supplements, ranging from 100 to 350 words each. Theo has three days before the deadline.

Theo writes the first supplement on a Friday night at 11 PM. The prompt is the standard _Why are you interested in our school?_ in 250 words. Theo opens with: _[School name] has captured my attention because of its unparalleled academic rigor, vibrant student community, and commitment to excellence in education._ Theo lists three programs from the website. Theo closes with: _I am confident that [School name] is the perfect fit for me._ Theo submits.

Theo writes the second supplement on Saturday morning. Same prompt, different school. Theo copies the structure of the first supplement, changes [School name] to the new school, swaps the three programs, and submits again. Two essays in two hours.

By Sunday afternoon, Theo has written all six supplements. The fifth and sixth are noticeably worse than the first. Theo is tired. The schools have started to blur. Theo has used the phrase _unparalleled academic rigor_ in three of the six essays. Theo notices the repetition only after the sixth submission and lies awake that night thinking about it.

This is the typical supplement-writing experience. It produces six generic essays, each of which fails the genre's specific demands. This chapter explains why and what to do instead.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: College Supplements (Why Us / Why You / Why This Major)
blocks.src:
### 4.2 What Admissions Readers Actually Do With Supplements

Janet, our reader from Chapters 1 and 3, returns. Janet reads supplements differently than she reads personal essays.

For the personal essay, Janet has the candidate's whole application open. She reads carefully if the opening earns reading. She is asking, _who is this candidate as a person?_

For the _Why this school_ supplement, Janet has a different question: _does this candidate know what they're getting into, and can they articulate why specifically here?_ Janet's reading is faster, typically two to four minutes per supplement, and her tolerance for generic language is lower. The supplement is a fit signal. A generic supplement signals _this candidate did not do their homework._ Janet does not need to read carefully to detect this. She can detect it in the first sentence.

The asymmetry: the personal essay asks Janet to evaluate the candidate as a writer and as a person. The supplement asks Janet to evaluate whether the candidate has done specific work to understand the school. Generic openings suggest no specific work was done. Janet's response to a generic supplement is not displeasure; it is _informed neutrality_ — she reads on, scans for any concrete fact, and downgrades her overall confidence in the candidate's fit.

On top of the universal pattern in §2.10, the supplement specifically requires:

  1. **A school-specific fact the candidate could only have learned by doing real research.** A course title plus a sentence on why that course's approach matters to the candidate; a faculty member plus a paper or teaching style the candidate has actually engaged with; a club plus a specific reason it would matter. _Not_ the school's slogan or brochure language.
  2. **A reciprocal fit claim.** What the school brings to the candidate _and_ what the candidate brings to the school. One-directional fit ("I want to go because it is excellent") reads as transactional; reciprocal fit signals the candidate has imagined themselves contributing, not just receiving.
  3. **The absence of brochure language.** _Vibrant community,_ _world-class faculty,_ _excellence in education,_ _unparalleled rigor,_ _cutting-edge research,_ _interdisciplinary opportunities_ — every one is brochure language. Janet has read each dozens of times this week. They do not signal effort; they signal copying.


### 4.3 Genre Conventions

The supplement has tighter conventions than the personal essay because it has tighter constraints — usually shorter word counts, more specific prompts, less room for narrative.


#### The Specificity Convention

The first sentence of a supplement should contain a fact about the school that the candidate could only have learned by doing research. Not the school's name in a flattering way; _a fact._

Bad: _Princeton's storied tradition and incomparable faculty have inspired me since I was young._

Bad: _I am drawn to Princeton because of its excellence in academic rigor._

Good: _Professor Eric Wieschaus's Modern Cell Biology course assigns a six-week independent research project I have been thinking about for the last year._

Good: _The Princeton Independent Concentration in Linguistic Computation does not exist as a major at any other school I am applying to, and I want it._

The good versions could only have been written by a candidate who looked at Princeton's actual course catalog or major list. The bad versions could be written about any school by any candidate.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: College Supplements (Why Us / Why You / Why This Major)
blocks.src:
#### The Reciprocal-Fit Convention

A successful supplement makes a two-directional claim. The candidate explains what the school offers that they need _and_ what they would bring to the school's community. One-directional supplements (just what the candidate gets from the school) sound transactional. Reciprocal supplements signal that the candidate has imagined themselves contributing to the campus, not just receiving from it.

The reciprocal claim does not need to be inflated. _I would bring my Saturday tutoring experience to the campus tutoring program_ is a reciprocal claim. _I would transform the campus through my unique perspective_ is the inflated version, which Janet recognizes immediately as performance.


#### The Recycling-Within-Limits Convention

Candidates writing six to twelve supplements in a season cannot write each from scratch. Some recycling is inevitable and even reasonable. The conventions of recycling:

* **Reusable** : a vignette about the candidate's specific past experience (a paragraph about Saturday tutoring, a paragraph about a research project, a paragraph about a family situation). These are facts about the candidate that do not change between schools.
* **Not reusable** : _anything_ that names the school. The school-specific paragraph must be written fresh for each school. The candidate who pastes the same school-specific paragraph into two supplements with [School name] swapped will be caught — sometimes by the reader, sometimes by accident (a leftover [School name] reference, a course code that does not exist at the new school).
* **Reusable with modification** : a thesis sentence about the candidate's intellectual orientation, modified slightly to align with the specific school's strengths.

The recycling matrix typically produces about 50 percent reused content and 50 percent fresh content per supplement. The fresh content is concentrated in the school-specific paragraphs and is the load-bearing material.


#### The Length Convention

Supplements have hard limits — 100, 150, 250, 350, 500 — that force compression. Going under is fine; 90 percent of the limit is normal; padding to exactly the limit produces flat sentences Janet can feel. See §15.4.1 for the consolidated cross-form reference.


#### The "Why This Major" Subtype

The "why this major" supplement is a distinct subtype with its own conventions. It is a curiosity test more than a fit test. Janet is asking: _does this candidate have a real intellectual relationship with this subject, or have they picked the major from a list of safe options?_

A successful "why this major" supplement contains:

* A specific intellectual encounter with the subject (a book, a problem, a class, a project, a conversation).
* A description of what the candidate finds interesting about the subject that a non-major would not necessarily say.
* A connection to the school's specific approach to the major (a course, a faculty member, a methodology).
* The absence of phrases like _I have always loved_ and _I am passionate about._


### 4.4 The 6 Moves Applied to Supplements

The 6 Moves operate slightly differently in supplements than in the personal essay because the supplement's reader, stakes, and format are different.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: College Supplements (Why Us / Why You / Why This Major)
blocks.src:
#### Move 1: Identify the Reader and Stakes

Janet reading a supplement is in a different mode than Janet reading a personal essay. The reader's question shifts from _who is this person?_ to _does this person know what they're getting into here?_ The candidate writing for the supplement-Janet should adopt a slightly different register: less narrative, more concrete, more compressed.


#### Move 2: Find the Specific Story (or the Specific Fact)

In supplements, Move 2 is often _find the Specific Fact about the school_ rather than _find the Specific Story about you._ The Specific Fact does the work the Specific Story does in the personal essay — it earns reading by signaling that the candidate has done particular work on this particular school.


#### Move 3: Open With a Hook That Earns Reading

The hook in a supplement is almost always the Specific Fact about the school. The first sentence should land a fact the candidate could only have learned by doing research. The personal-essay hook (a Specific Object placed in motion) is sometimes possible in longer supplements but rarely in 100- or 150-word supplements.


#### Move 4: Show With Specifics

Specific facts about the school + specific facts about the candidate. A supplement should contain at least two of each: two specific things about the school, two specific things about the candidate. In a 100-word supplement, that may compress to one of each.


#### Move 5: Connect Specifics to Claims

The connection in a supplement is usually the _reciprocal-fit_ sentence — the sentence that says what the candidate would bring to the school in return. The connection is more direct than in the personal essay because space is tight.


#### Move 6: Survive the AI Test

Supplements are the form most vulnerable to AI generation. A model given the prompt _write a why-Princeton supplement for a candidate interested in computer science_ will produce something fluent, organized, and indistinguishable from the AI output of every other applicant. The AI test for supplements is harsher: _if I removed all proper nouns and specific facts, would the supplement read identically to one for any other school?_ If yes, the supplement has not survived the AI test, regardless of how polished the prose is.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: College Supplements (Why Us / Why You / Why This Major)
blocks.src:
### 4.5 Theo's Supplements Revised

Theo, after the Sunday-night reckoning, returns to the six supplements before the deadline and applies the 6 Moves. The first supplement, in its original form:

> [School name] has captured my attention because of its unparalleled academic rigor, vibrant student community, and commitment to excellence in education. I am especially excited about the Computer Science department, the Economics department, and the Philosophy department, each of which offers world-class programs. I am confident that [School name] is the perfect fit for me.

Run the 6 Moves: Move 1 failed (no fit signal, just brochure language); Move 2 failed (no Specific Fact about the school); Move 3 failed (the opening contains no hook); Move 4 failed (zero specifics); Move 5 failed (no reciprocal claim); Move 6 catastrophically failed (this supplement could be generated by an AI in two seconds).

Theo discards the supplement and writes a new one. The school is the University of Chicago. Theo has spent an actual hour reading the Chicago website. Theo has noticed the Common Core, has looked at the political science department's faculty list, and has read the description of the Big Problems Curriculum.

> The University of Chicago is the only school on my application list that requires a sequence in Civilization Studies. I have been reading the Iliad on my own this fall, slowly, in three different translations, because I wanted to understand what changes when a translator changes one verb. I would not have done this for fun if I were not the kind of person who would also enjoy reading Hobbes and Mill in the same room with twenty other people who chose the same sequence. The Big Problems Curriculum's seminar on cooperation seems written for the way I have been thinking about my Saturday job at the tutoring center, where the eight-year-olds we work with cannot yet read but already have rules for sharing the carrots at snack time. I would bring those rules into the seminar.

Run the 6 Moves on this new supplement:

* **Move 1** : Done. Janet reads this and instantly registers _this candidate has done work._
