* **Move 2** : Done. Specific Fact: the Civilization Studies sequence; the Big Problems Curriculum seminar on cooperation.
* **Move 3** : Done. The first sentence states a Specific Fact (Chicago is the only school requiring this sequence). The reader continues.
* **Move 4** : Done. Specific Objects: three translations of the _Iliad,_ Hobbes, Mill, the Saturday job, the eight-year-olds, the carrots at snack time.
* **Move 5** : Done. The reciprocal-fit sentence is the closing — _I would bring those rules into the seminar._ Theo brings something specific (the eight-year-olds' carrot rules) to a specific seminar (Big Problems on cooperation).
* **Move 6** : Done. No AI given a generic Chicago prompt would have produced the carrot-rule connection. The specific hour Theo spent on the _Iliad_ and the specific tutoring detail are unique to Theo.

The 195-word version is stronger than the original 250-word version. Theo cuts 55 words and ships.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: College Supplements (Why Us / Why You / Why This Major)
blocks.src:
### 4.6 A Complete Sample: Two Supplements for Two Schools

Below are two supplements written by the same applicant — a high school senior in St. Louis, applying as a prospective biology major, who has worked in a community garden for three years. The point of showing two from one candidate is to demonstrate that the same person writes different supplements when they think specifically about what each school offers, rather than paste-and-swap.


#### Supplement 1: Cornell University, "Why this major?" (250 words)

> Last spring, I noticed that the kale in our community garden's south plot was getting a fungal infection while the kale in the north plot — twelve feet away, same soil mix, same seed — was fine. I spent four Saturdays trying to figure out why. The answer turned out to be airflow: the south plot was on the leeward side of an old fence the community board had built without thinking about ventilation. I learned this from a county extension agent who took my call seriously when she should not have had to.
> 
> What I discovered, beyond the fungus answer, is that I want to spend a long time learning the small ways living things respond to small changes in their environments. Cornell's PLBIO 2410 (_Plant Pathology_) is the course I have been waiting for the chance to take. I have read the syllabus on the public website three times. The unit on biological control agents is exactly the question I had about the kale that I could not yet ask precisely.
> 
> I also want, eventually, to have the question-asking ability of the extension agent who answered my call. Cornell's New York State Integrated Pest Management Program is, as far as I can tell, the place that ability gets institutionalized. I would bring my four Saturdays of fungus research and my three years of community-garden teaching with elementary school groups to whichever lab would have me.

This is a good "why this major" supplement. It contains a Specific Story (the kale; the four Saturdays; the extension agent), Specific Facts about Cornell (PLBIO 2410, the IPM program), and a reciprocal-fit sentence at the end. It survives the AI test — the kale-airflow story is not generic.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: College Supplements (Why Us / Why You / Why This Major)
blocks.src:
#### Supplement 2: Brown University, "Why us?" (250 words)

> Brown's Open Curriculum is one of two reasons my list includes Brown. The other is BIOL 0480 (_The Biology of Race and Health_), which I read about in a profile of Professor Lundy Braun. The course's framing of medical history, that the categories medical research has used to organize patients have themselves shaped what medicine can see — is the question I have been trying to articulate while volunteering at a free clinic on Cherokee Street.
> 
> The clinic serves mostly Bosnian and Vietnamese immigrants. I have noticed, over the last year, that the intake form's race categories are not categories the patients themselves use, and the doctors are quietly translating both directions. I do not yet know what this means. The Open Curriculum would let me find out — by combining BIOL 0480 with a course in medical anthropology and another in epidemiology, taken in the order that the question requires rather than the order a fixed major would dictate.
> 
> What I would bring to Brown is a year of intake-form questions and a habit of rephrasing a question until I can ask it precisely. I do not yet know precisely what I am asking. I would like four years to figure out.

This supplement does the same work in a different register. Specific Facts about Brown: the Open Curriculum, BIOL 0480, Professor Braun. Specific Story about the candidate: the Cherokee Street clinic, the intake form, the Bosnian and Vietnamese immigrants. Reciprocal claim: _what I would bring to Brown._ Survives the AI test.

Notice that the two supplements share _no language_ but share the same underlying logic. The applicant wrote about the same candidate (themselves) for two different schools, with each school's specific supplements doing different specific work. There is no paste-and-swap. There is only a candidate who has thought about what each school specifically offers and written toward that.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: College Supplements (Why Us / Why You / Why This Major)
blocks.src:
### 4.7 Common Pitfalls

**Pitfall 1: The brochure echo.** The candidate writes back to the school in the school's own marketing language. _The vibrant intellectual community_ and _world-class faculty_ are direct echoes of the school's website. Janet recognizes the echo immediately and discounts the candidate. The remedy: read the website only to extract specific facts; do not absorb the website's language.

**Pitfall 2: The course-list dump.** The candidate lists five courses they want to take without saying anything specific about why those particular courses. Course-list dumps signal browsing, not engagement. The remedy: pick one or two courses and say something specific about each — what the candidate has been thinking that this course would help them think more clearly.

**Pitfall 3: The faculty-name-drop.** The candidate names a faculty member without engaging with anything specific the faculty member has done. _I look forward to working with Professor X_ is a name-drop. _Professor X's 2018 paper on Y is the framing I have been missing in my own thinking about Z_ is engagement. Engagement requires that the candidate actually read something the faculty member wrote, which most candidates do not bother to do.

**Pitfall 4: The paste-and-swap betrayal.** The candidate copies the same supplement to two schools, swapping [School name]. The reader catches it because of a leftover phrase, an inconsistent course code, or simply the smell of recycled prose. The remedy: do not paste-and-swap. Reuse vignettes about yourself; rewrite school-specific paragraphs from scratch.

**Pitfall 5: The "perfect fit" close.** The candidate closes with _I am confident that X is the perfect fit for me._ This sentence is on the implicit _do not_ list. It is generic. It is over-confident. It is something every other candidate has written. The remedy: close with a specific image or a specific reciprocal claim — a sentence that could not have closed any other supplement.


### 4.8 The Recycling Matrix

A candidate writing eight supplements over four weeks needs a workflow. The recycling matrix is one approach.

Block | Reusable? | Notes  
---|---|---  
Personal vignette (50–80 words) | Yes, with light edits | Saturday tutoring; community garden; family financial setback. Each vignette is true; reusing is not lying.  
Intellectual orientation paragraph (40–60 words) | Yes, with school-specific tail | The candidate's general orientation; the tail names a specific course or faculty connection.  
School-specific facts paragraph (60–100 words) | No | Must be fresh per school. The most labor-intensive part.  
Reciprocal-fit sentence (20–40 words) | Sometimes | Reusable if the candidate's contribution is school-independent (e.g., _I would bring my Saturday tutoring_); fresh if the contribution is specific to the school's programs.  
Closing image or claim (15–30 words) | Usually fresh | Generic closes are detectable; specific closes are short and worth the effort.  
  
The recycling matrix produces, on average, 40–60% reused content and 40–60% fresh content per supplement. The fresh content is concentrated in the school-specific paragraph, where it carries the supplement's load.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: College Supplements (Why Us / Why You / Why This Major)
blocks.src:
### 4.9 Cultural and ESL Calibration

ESL candidates writing supplements face a specific compounded challenge. The supplement's fit claim is culturally weighted: it asks the candidate to position themselves _toward_ the school in a way that signals cultural fluency with the school's intellectual traditions. Candidates from educational systems that do not encourage students to engage critically with universities (i.e., to consider whether _they_ fit _the school_ rather than only whether _the school_ will accept _them_) may default to flattering the school in the wrong register.

The remedy is the same as in Chapter 3: study the school as you would study any specific institution with its own peculiarities. Read its course catalog, its faculty pages, its student newspaper. Find facts the school's own marketing does not lead with. The "Why this school" essay is a research exercise as much as a writing exercise; ESL candidates often write _better_ supplements than native speakers because they have done more research, having less prior intuition about American universities to fall back on.


### 4.10 Reader Draft Prompt

Pick one school you are applying to (or considering). Spend forty-five uninterrupted minutes on the school's website. Read three faculty pages, three course descriptions, the requirements for your intended major, and the student newspaper's most recent issue. Write down three specific facts about the school that you could not have known before this research session.

Now write a 150-word "why this school" paragraph. The paragraph should contain at least two of your three specific facts and one specific thing about you that connects to one of those facts.

Save the paragraph. We will return to it in Chapter 17.


### 4.11 Exercises


#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Why does Janet read supplements differently from personal essays?

**Answer:** Janet reads personal essays asking _who is this person?_ She reads supplements asking _does this person know what they're getting into here?_ The supplement is a fit signal, and Janet's tolerance for generic language is lower because generic supplements indicate the candidate did no specific research. Reading time per supplement is also shorter (2–4 minutes vs. 6–7 for the personal essay).

**Q2.** Define the reciprocal-fit convention.

**Answer:** A successful supplement makes a two-directional claim — what the school offers the candidate _and_ what the candidate would bring to the school. One-directional supplements (only what the candidate gets) sound transactional. Reciprocal supplements signal that the candidate has imagined themselves as a contributor to the campus, not just a recipient.

**Q3.** What language should be avoided in supplement openings?

**Answer:** Brochure language echoed back from the school's website — _vibrant community, world-class faculty, excellence in education, unparalleled rigor, cutting-edge research, interdisciplinary opportunities, storied tradition, perfect fit._ Each phrase appears in marketing copy and is recognized immediately as recycled rather than original.

**Q4.** What is the AI-test for supplements specifically?

**Answer:** _If I removed all proper nouns and specific facts, would the supplement read identically to one for any other school?_ If yes, the supplement has not survived the AI test. The asymmetric demand for supplements is that they should contain school-specific content that is structurally non-portable.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: College Supplements (Why Us / Why You / Why This Major)
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1. Diagnose this opening.**

> Stanford has captured my imagination since I was a young child. Its commitment to academic excellence, its world-class faculty, and its vibrant student community make it the ideal place for me to pursue my passion for computer science.

Run the 6 Moves and identify the pitfalls.

Hint

This opening commits at least three of the named pitfalls.

**Answer:** Move 1 failed (no school-specific work signaled). Move 2 failed (no Specific Fact about Stanford; the named features apply to any selective school). Move 3 failed (the _captured my imagination since I was a young child_ phrasing is on the implicit do-not list). Move 4 failed (zero Specific Objects). Move 6 failed (an AI given the prompt _write a Why-Stanford supplement for a CS applicant_ would produce exactly this).

Pitfalls committed: brochure echo (_vibrant student community, world-class faculty, academic excellence_); the "perfect fit" close (here in the opening as _the ideal place for me_); the always-having claim (_captured my imagination since I was a young child_).

**Q2. Rewrite this supplement using two specific Stanford facts.**

A candidate is applying to Stanford as a prospective CS major. They have done a summer Python project building a small recommendation engine for their school library. Write a 200-word _why Stanford_ supplement that uses at least two specific Stanford-only facts (you may invent plausible specific facts: a specific course code with title, a specific faculty member's research direction, a specific feature of Stanford's CS curriculum). The supplement should pass all six moves.

Hint

The candidate's library-project vignette is reusable. The Stanford facts are not.

**Answer:**

> Stanford CS 224W (_Machine Learning with Graphs_) is the course I would not be ready for if I applied next year, and I want the year of preparation it would take. My summer recommendation engine for my school library did the easy part, content-based filtering on book metadata, and broke when I tried to model what 320 patrons borrowed in what sequence over two years. The graphs version is what I could not figure out. Professor Leskovec's lecture notes (which I have read in pieces, mostly the parts I could mostly understand) are the closest thing I have found to a textbook for the question I was actually trying to ask. Stanford's CURIS program is the second reason I am applying: I want to do, with someone else's supervision, the kind of project I tried to do alone last summer. I would bring back to the library, both the Stanford library and my school library, whatever recommendation engine the next attempt produces. I would also like to take the metadata I have already collected to a faculty member who would know what to do with it.

This passes all six moves: Move 1 (Janet reads the candidate as having done specific work), Move 2 (the Specific Story is the broken recommendation engine), Move 3 (CS 224W is a Specific Fact placed in motion), Move 4 (six Specific Objects: 224W, 320 patrons, Professor Leskovec's lecture notes, CURIS, the school library, the metadata), Move 5 (the reciprocal-fit sentence about bringing the engine back), Move 6 (the broken-engine vignette is not generic).

**Q3. Insert one Specific Object that you actually hold.**

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: College Supplements (Why Us / Why You / Why This Major)
blocks.src:
Below is a generic supplement opening — the kind that could belong to any candidate. Rewrite it so that one Specific Object you (the reader) genuinely own, have used, have read, or have built in the past year anchors the opening. The Object should be nameable in a phrase ("a green plastic Saturday-school radio," "the second-edition copy of _Norwegian Wood_ my aunt mailed me"). Keep the rewrite to about 80 words.

> Princeton's emphasis on undergraduate research and small-class discussion is what draws me. I have always loved the intersection of literature and history, and I am looking for a program that lets me explore both rigorously. Princeton's reputation for producing thoughtful, engaged graduates makes it the natural place for me to spend the next four years.

Hint

Pick an Object that is on your desk, in your bag, or in your phone's photo roll right now. The Object should carry your fingerprints — something a different candidate could not have written about. If the Object is a book, name the edition and what page you are stuck on. If a tool, name the project it has been on.

**Answer:** Answers will vary; the discipline is in whether the Object is genuinely yours. A passing rewrite:

> The history of the Atlantic slave trade I am currently reading — Marcus Rediker's _The Slave Ship,_ the copy with the brittle library-sale sticker still on the spine — has me stuck on the chapter about the ship's surgeons, because I do not yet have the vocabulary to argue with it. Princeton's HIS 388 with Professor Sandra Greene is where I would learn the vocabulary. I would also bring back to Princeton's Africana Studies reading room the marginalia I have been keeping in the back of the Rediker.

The rewrite earns the read because the Object (the specific Rediker copy, with its sale sticker) is one this candidate alone could have placed on the page. The next round of revision should add a second Princeton-specific fact; the Object has done the harder work of making the opening _theirs_.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: College Supplements (Why Us / Why You / Why This Major)
blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** The chapter argues that the supplement is often the deciding factor between two comparable applicants. Yet many applicants treat the supplements as last-minute work. Explain the gap. Why do candidates underweight a form that admissions readers weight so heavily?

**Discussion:** Several explanations are partly true. The personal essay is more emotionally salient — it feels like the _real_ essay, while supplements feel like paperwork. Candidates overestimate the marginal effect of the personal essay and underestimate the supplements'. By the eighth or twelfth supplement, cognitive bandwidth has run out. High school counselors often emphasize the personal essay disproportionately, reinforcing the misallocation. The chapter's claim is empirical: at the margin, in committee, the supplements decide. The candidate who allocates effort to match the deciding factor outperforms peers who allocate by emotional salience.

**Q2.** Recycling supplements is officially discouraged. In practice, almost all candidates do some recycling. Where is the line between _reasonable recycling_ and _paste-and-swap betrayal_?

**Discussion:** The line is roughly: reuse content about _yourself_ that does not change between schools (a vignette about Saturday tutoring, a paragraph about your intellectual orientation). Do not reuse content about the _school_ that should change between schools (specific courses, faculty members, programs). The deeper test: if you remove school names from the recycled portion, does it still read coherently? If yes, it is reasonable recycling. If the recycled portion contains course codes or faculty names that have to be swapped, it is paste-and-swap and likely to be detected. The book's stronger claim: the school-specific paragraph should be written from scratch each time, no exceptions.

**Q3.** The "why this major" supplement is a curiosity test. Some majors are easier to demonstrate curiosity for than others. A candidate applying as a CS major can point to coding projects; a candidate applying as a history major has fewer obvious props. How should the candidate for a less-prop-heavy major demonstrate curiosity?

**Discussion:** Reading is the universal prop. A candidate who has read three books about a historical period and can articulate what each one missed has demonstrated curiosity. So has one who has visited an archive, read a primary source in translation, written an unassigned research paper, or attended a free public lecture. Every academic discipline has _some_ artifact a curious 17-year-old can produce. The candidate who has not produced one is not yet ready to claim the major; the candidate who has should describe it specifically. The "why this major" supplement is partly a filter — it surfaces who has done their own work and who has only filled out forms.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 4: College Supplements (Why Us / Why You / Why This Major)
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

The supplement is the form most candidates underweight and most admissions readers weight heavily. Its convention is specificity: specific facts about the school that the candidate could only have learned by doing real research, paired with specific facts about the candidate that connect to those facts. Brochure language is the dominant pitfall; the AI test is harsher for supplements than for the personal essay.

The recycling matrix allows reasonable reuse of personal vignettes while keeping school-specific paragraphs fresh per school. The reciprocal-fit convention asks the candidate to claim what they would bring to the school's community, not only what the school would do for them.

The next chapter (Chapter 5) treats the graduate personal statement, where Janet is replaced by a graduate-program faculty committee with a different reading question altogether: not _who is this person?_ but _what research direction is this person prepared to pursue?_

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: The Graduate School Personal Statement
blocks.src:
Graduate readers read for evidence of a research direction more than for personality. A vivid childhood story without a research question is a category error.

This is the central reorientation of Part II. The reader of a graduate personal statement is not Janet on her sofa at 11 PM. The reader is Professor Lay, the graduate admissions chair of a master's program in cognitive science, reading on a Saturday morning in February at her office, with the eighteenth statement of the morning open in her browser, a cup of green tea cooling, and a sheet of yellow legal-pad paper next to the keyboard on which she is writing one-line summaries of each candidate's research interests. _Eighteenth, attention and decision-making, fMRI methods, may match Tomasi in the lab next door._

Professor Lay is not asking who you are as a person. She is asking what research question you arrive prepared to pursue and whether her department is the place to pursue it. The graduate personal statement is a different genre from the college essay, and most candidates discover this by writing the wrong one first.


### 5.1 Vignette: Theo Drafts a Graduate Statement

Theo, three years older than in the previous chapters, is now a junior in college majoring in cognitive science. Theo is applying to master's programs in cognitive science with an eye toward eventually pursuing a PhD. The application requires a 1,000-word personal statement.

Theo's first draft begins:

> Ever since I was a child, I have been fascinated by the human mind. Growing up as the granddaughter of a Salvadoran immigrant, I was particularly curious about how language shapes thought. As an undergraduate at State University, I have pursued this curiosity through coursework in linguistics, psychology, and computer science.

Theo writes this draft on a Tuesday night and shows it to a junior research advisor on Wednesday. The advisor, who has read several hundred graduate statements over a decade of admissions service, returns it with one comment in red pen: _Cut everything before paragraph 3._

Theo is confused. Theo's college essay had begun similarly, with a personal anchor, and had worked. The advisor explains: this is a different reader. Professor Lay does not need the childhood anchor. Professor Lay needs the research question.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: The Graduate School Personal Statement
blocks.src:
### 5.2 What Graduate Readers Actually Do

Professor Lay's process for reading a graduate personal statement, repeated with minor variations across hundreds of statements per cycle:

  1. **Read the first paragraph carefully.** She is looking for: a research question articulated specifically; evidence the candidate has done research-relevant work; an indication of methodological orientation. (About 60 seconds.)
  2. **Skim the middle paragraphs for evidence.** She looks for: prior research projects, methods used, results obtained, what the candidate learned from each. (About 3–5 minutes.)
  3. **Read the fit paragraph carefully.** She looks for: specific faculty members named with specific reasons; specific methodological approaches the department offers that match the candidate's goals. (About 60–90 seconds.)
  4. **Read the closing carefully.** She looks for: a clear statement of what the candidate hopes to do during the program; an honest acknowledgment of what the candidate does not yet know. (About 30 seconds.)

The total reading time per statement is 8 to 15 minutes — roughly twice the reading time of an undergraduate essay. The asymmetry: undergraduate readers are evaluating who you are; graduate readers are evaluating who you are _as a researcher._ The latter requires more reading because it requires more evidence.

Layered on top of the universal pattern in §2.10, Professor Lay specifically expects:

  1. **A research question, specifically stated.** Not _I am interested in cognition_ — that is a topic. A question: _I want to understand how attentional control develops between ages 4 and 8 and whether the developmental trajectory differs in bilingual versus monolingual children._ The question may be wrong and revised within the first semester, but the candidate who can articulate one is recognizably different from the candidate who can name only a topic.
  2. **Methodological awareness.** The candidate knows what kinds of methods are used to address what kinds of questions. Behavioral, fMRI, and computational modeling candidates are different animals. A candidate who does not yet know which methodological camp they belong to is fine, _as long as they say so honestly_ and do not pretend.
  3. **Department-specific fit.** Faculty named with specific reasons. Programs of study within the department named with specific reasons. The fit signal is genuine only when it could not have been written about another department.

Professor Lay specifically discounts:

  1. **Personal narrative for its own sake.** A two-page family story without research relevance is a category error. (A short personal anchor that motivates a research question is fine; the unanchored personal narrative is not.)
  2. **Coursework as achievement.** That the candidate took advanced classes is on the transcript. The statement should describe what the candidate _did_ with the coursework, not which courses they took.


### 5.3 Genre Conventions

The graduate personal statement has accreted conventions that differ from the undergraduate genre.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: The Graduate School Personal Statement
blocks.src:
#### The Research-Question Opener

The first paragraph of a graduate statement should articulate a research question or, at minimum, a research direction with enough specificity that the reader can place the candidate methodologically and topically. The childhood-anchor opener of the undergraduate essay is wrong here. Two acceptable variants of the research-question opener:

**Variant 1: The direct question opener.**

> I want to understand how working memory capacity constrains second-language acquisition in adults and whether the constraint is structural or strategic. The question came into focus during my junior-year independent study with Professor Liu, where I built a behavioral paradigm to test working-memory load in 32 native-English-speaking adults learning a small artificial vocabulary in Mandarin tonal contrasts.

**Variant 2: The research-encounter opener.**

> The first time I read the Saffran-Aslin-Newport infant statistical-learning experiments, I was a sophomore in an intro cognitive science class and could not stop thinking about whether the same paradigm would work in adult L2 learners. I have since spent two years trying to find out.

Both variants do the work the childhood anchor does in the undergraduate essay (signal who you are) without performing the personal-narrative register that does not fit the graduate context.


#### The Evidence-Forward Body

The body of the graduate statement is _evidence-forward._ The candidate names specific projects, specific methods, specific results, and specific things learned. The evidence is concrete. The proportion of statement devoted to evidence is roughly 50–60% — substantially more than in the undergraduate essay, where the proportion devoted to a single Specific Story might be 60–70%.

Each piece of evidence should answer four questions:

  1. What was the question being investigated?
  2. What did the candidate specifically do?
  3. What was the result, and what did the candidate learn from it (including from the parts that did not work)?
  4. How does this lead to the candidate's current research interest?

A 1,000-word statement typically has room for two or three pieces of evidence developed at this depth, plus a brief gesture toward additional pieces.


#### The Fit Paragraph

The fit paragraph names specific faculty members and specific reasons. The conventions:

* Name two to three faculty members, not one and not five. One signals over-reliance on a single advisor; five signals lack of focus.
* For each named faculty member, give a specific reason — a paper, a methodological approach, a project the candidate has read about. _Professor Smith's 2021 paper on phonological processing in early bilinguals frames a question I have been pursuing since my honors thesis_ is engagement. _Professor Smith's research on bilingualism_ is not.
* Name one or two methodological resources the department has, a specific lab facility, a specific data set, a specific course sequence, that the candidate would use.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: The Graduate School Personal Statement
blocks.src:
#### The Closing

The closing of a graduate statement is forward-looking and honest. Forward-looking: what the candidate hopes to do during the master's program. Honest: an acknowledgment that the candidate's current research interest may evolve and that the candidate is open to that evolution.

The closing convention to avoid: claiming with confidence that one already knows exactly what one will work on for two years. Graduate committees know that two-year predictions are rarely accurate. The candidate who claims certainty signals naivety. The candidate who acknowledges uncertainty signals readiness for the actual research process.


### 5.4 The 6 Moves Applied


#### Move 1: The Reader

Professor Lay reading on a Saturday morning. She is looking for a researcher, not a person. The personal essay's emotional vulnerability is out of place; the supplement's institutional fit is partly relevant; what is fully relevant is the candidate's research orientation.


#### Move 2: The Specific "Story"

In the graduate statement, the Specific Story is usually a research story. A specific project the candidate worked on. A specific question that emerged from the project. A specific result that did or did not work. The story is intellectually concrete, not emotionally concrete.


#### Move 3: The Hook

The hook is the research question. It should appear in the first two sentences, in specific form. The hook may also be a research-encounter moment — the first time the candidate read a particular paper or attended a particular lab meeting and registered the question.


#### Move 4: Show With Specifics

Specifics in a graduate statement are: paradigms, data sets, methods, results, papers read, faculty engaged with. The Specific Object Test still applies, but the _kind_ of specific object shifts. _320 hours of video,_ _the bilingual subgroup,_ _Professor Liu's behavioral paradigm,_ _32 adult learners,_ _Mandarin tonal contrasts_ — these are the Specific Objects of the graduate genre.


#### Move 5: Connect Specifics to Claims

The claim being supported is _I am ready to do research at this level._ The specifics support the claim by demonstrating, not asserting, research-readiness. The Restrained Connection from Chapter 2 still applies: do not claim _and from this experience I learned the importance of careful experimental design._ Show the careful experimental design and let the reader infer the learning.


#### Move 6: Survive the AI Test

Graduate statements are highly vulnerable to AI generation. An AI given a research topic and a candidate background can produce a fluent-sounding statement quickly. The AI test for graduate statements: _if I removed the specific names of papers, projects, faculty, and methods, would the statement read identically to one for any other candidate in this subfield?_ If yes, the statement has not survived. The remedy is concrete specifics — paper titles read, exact paradigms used, exact data set sizes, exact unsolved problems encountered.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: The Graduate School Personal Statement
blocks.src:
### 5.5 Theo's Revised Statement

Theo, after the advisor's red-pen comment, returns to the statement. Theo cuts everything before paragraph 3. The new opening:

> The question I am applying to graduate school to pursue is whether the well-documented bilingual advantage in attentional control is robust across socioeconomic strata or partly a confound. The question reaches further back than the lab work I will describe: I grew up watching my grandmother keep an AM Spanish-language station on in the kitchen long after she had stopped speaking Spanish at home, and I spent a summer trying to learn enough Salvadoran Spanish to ask her why. The pivot from that summer to a behavioral paradigm took two years of coursework. Last summer, working in Professor Ramirez's lab, I helped collect Stroop-task data on 156 bilingual children aged 6–9, drawn from two community partners — 78 in a high-income school district, 78 in a low-income district. The bilingual advantage replicated in the high-income subsample (Cohen's d = 0.42) and disappeared in the low-income subsample (d = 0.04). I do not yet know what to make of this. I want to spend the next two years finding out.

Run the 6 Moves on the new opening:

* **Move 1** : Done. Professor Lay reads this and instantly registers a candidate with a research question and prior data.
* **Move 2** : Done. The Specific Research Story (the summer project; the 156 children; the divergent results) is the spine.
* **Move 3** : Done. The first sentence states the research question concretely. The reader continues for the resolution.
* **Move 4** : Done. Specific Objects: the AM Spanish-language station in the grandmother's kitchen, Professor Ramirez's lab, the Stroop task, 156 children (78 high-income, 78 low-income), the two community partners, the effect sizes, _bilingual advantage_.
* **Move 5** : Done with restraint. _I do not yet know what to make of this. I want to spend the next two years finding out_ is connection without over-claiming. The two-sentence personal anchor (the grandmother and the Spanish-language station) does the §5.7 personal-anchor convention well: brief, immediately tied to the research question, and followed by the research evidence within the same paragraph.
* **Move 6** : Done. The specific data, 156 children, two community partners, effect sizes, could not have been produced by an AI given a generic prompt.

The new opening is 130 words. The remaining 870 words of the statement develop the evidence (two more research projects), the methodological orientation, the fit paragraph naming three faculty, and the closing. The full statement passes all six moves.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: The Graduate School Personal Statement
blocks.src:
### 5.6 A Complete Sample Graduate Statement

Below is a complete statement (~950 words) by a fictional applicant, Wen, applying to a master's program in computational linguistics.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: The Graduate School Personal Statement
blocks.src:
> The question I am applying to study is whether large language models acquire syntactic knowledge that generalizes across typologically distinct languages, or whether they acquire surface-level patterns that masquerade as syntactic knowledge in high-resource languages and break down in low-resource ones. The question came into focus during my senior thesis with Professor Park, in which we evaluated GPT-2's performance on subject-verb agreement in Korean — a language with rich agglutinative morphology that is typologically distant from English. The model's accuracy on long-distance agreement dropped from 89% on simple matrix clauses to 31% on embedded clauses with intervening adjuncts. The 31% is roughly chance for our paradigm. The drop is not specific to GPT-2; we replicated it in two open-source multilingual models.
> 
> I want to understand whether the drop reflects a fundamental limit in current architectures or an artifact of training-data imbalance. The two hypotheses make different predictions for low-resource Indo-European languages with similar typology to Korean (e.g., Hungarian, Finnish), and we currently have data only for Korean. The natural next step is a typologically broader paradigm, which is what I would propose to do in graduate school.
> 
> My research preparation has three components. First, the senior thesis described above, which produced a paper currently in revision for the _International Conference on Computational Linguistics_ student session and which I will present at our department's research symposium in March. Second, two summers in Professor Park's lab, including a summer of paradigm development with five Korean-speaking participants in pilot work. Third, coursework in formal syntax (LING 401), computational linguistics (LING 480), and graduate-level statistics (STAT 540), the last of which I took because the lab's analysis pipeline relied on mixed-effects logistic regression I had not understood from textbook readings alone.
> 
> The methodological orientation I bring is mixed: I am comfortable with behavioral evaluation paradigms (the senior thesis used both targeted minimal-pair tests and naturalistic context evaluation), I have working but not advanced facility with PyTorch and HuggingFace, and I am beginning to learn probing-based interpretability methods. I do not yet know how to do mechanistic interpretability, the recent work coming out of Anthropic and others, and I would like to learn it.
> 
> The University of Washington's Computational Linguistics program is the program I am most excited to apply to for three specific reasons. First, Professor Bender's work on the Bender Rule and on responsible LLM evaluation has shaped how I framed the typological-generalization question; the Korean-to-English asymmetry I observed is exactly the kind of imbalance her work argues we should test for. Second, Professor Smith's work on syntactic probing methods would directly extend the behavioral paradigms I have used so far into more direct measurements of model internals. Third, the program's relationship with the Allen Institute for AI provides access to model evaluations at scale that would not be feasible at most universities, and the multilingual data resources held within the institute include several of the low-resource languages my proposed extension would require.
> 
> I would also bring useful prior work to the program. The Korean evaluation paradigm developed in Professor Park's lab is generalizable to other agglutinative languages with morphologically marked agreement; I have written documentation that could serve as a starting point for collaborators interested in extending it. My data-cleaning code for handling Korean honorific agreement (a non-trivial preprocessing problem) is on GitHub and has been used by two other students in the lab.
> 
> Two acknowledgments belong in this statement. First, my research interest may shift during the master's program; the typological-generalization question is the most specific version of a broader interest in the limits of current language models, and I expect to revise the specific question as I learn more. Second, I do not yet know whether I will pursue a PhD after the master's. I want the master's to help me find out — both by doing more research and by working closely enough with faculty that I can evaluate honestly whether I am suited for a longer research career.
> 
> What I hope to do in the program: complete a master's thesis that extends the typological-generalization paradigm to Hungarian and Finnish (with possible expansion to a Slavic language depending on data availability), present at one major conference, and contribute to one collaborative project outside my thesis topic. I would also like to take the program's seminar in interpretability methods (the one Professor Smith teaches in the fall), even though it is outside my immediate thesis methodology, because I expect the question of _what models actually know_ to remain central to my work for the rest of my career.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: The Graduate School Personal Statement
blocks.src:
This statement is approximately 950 words and does what the genre requires:

* Opens with a research question (Move 3 done in research register).
* Develops three pieces of evidence (the senior thesis with specific results; two summers in the lab; specific coursework with specific reasons).
* Names methodological orientation honestly, including what the candidate does not yet know.
* Names three faculty with specific reasons (Move 1 + Move 4 done in research register).
* Closes with concrete plans and honest acknowledgments.
* Survives the AI test: the 89% / 31% accuracy drop, the Korean-English asymmetry, the specific paradigm, the GitHub documentation are all specific to Wen.

The statement is dense. It does not have time for a childhood anchor, an emotional reflection, or an inflated phrase about the importance of language. It is a research document with a specific candidate behind it. That is the genre.


#### A Note on Recommendation Letters for Graduate Applications

Graduate applications typically require two or three letters of recommendation. The brag sheet from §13.5 — a one-to-three-page document of specific projects, specific moments, and what the application asks the recommender to address — applies here. For graduate applications specifically, the brag sheet should orient the recommender toward the research-direction question your statement opens with, not toward general accomplishments.


### 5.7 Common Pitfalls

**Pitfall 1: The college-essay register.** A candidate writes a graduate statement in the register of an undergraduate personal essay — long childhood anchor, emotional reflection, inflated language about the field. The statement is well-written but in the wrong genre. Professor Lay registers it as _not yet ready for the graduate-level conversation._

**Pitfall 2: The unanchored research interest.** The candidate names a research interest without evidence of having done relevant prior work. _I am interested in cognitive neuroscience_ is not an interest; it is a topic. The remedy: anchor the interest to a specific project, paper read, or experience. If no anchor exists, the candidate may not yet be ready to claim the interest.

**Pitfall 3: The course-list dump.** The candidate lists every advanced class taken without describing what was _done_ in the classes. The transcript already shows the courses. The statement should describe specific work, papers written, projects completed, problems engaged with, not the catalogue of courses.

**Pitfall 4: The faculty-name-drop without engagement.** The candidate names three faculty members without saying anything specific about each. _I would like to work with Professor X, Professor Y, and Professor Z_ is name-dropping. _Professor X's 2020 paper on Y is the methodological framework I have been trying to apply_ is engagement.

**Pitfall 5: The over-confident closing.** The candidate claims to know exactly what they will work on for the next two or six years. Graduate committees know two-year predictions are rarely accurate; six-year predictions almost never are. The remedy: state plans concretely while acknowledging that the specific question will likely evolve.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: The Graduate School Personal Statement
blocks.src:
### 5.8 Cultural and ESL Calibration

The graduate statement's research-forward register is, in some ways, _easier_ for ESL applicants than the undergraduate essay's emotional register. The graduate genre rewards specificity, precision, and methodological clarity — qualities that many international educational systems train more rigorously than the U.S. system trains emotional vulnerability.

The challenge for ESL applicants is different: it is to ensure that the statement does not read as a translated CV. Some international academic traditions emphasize listing accomplishments more than narrating intellectual development. The U.S. graduate statement asks for the latter — what the candidate is _thinking,_ not only what the candidate has _done._ The remedy is to ensure that each piece of evidence in the statement is followed by a sentence about what the candidate _learned_ or _began to wonder_ as a result.

For non-native English writers specifically: the statement may benefit from a careful read by a native or near-native speaker for sentence-level clarity. The conventions of academic English in the U.S. tradition (active voice, concrete verbs, short sentences) are not universal. Local academic English in some countries uses longer sentences, more passive constructions, and more nominalizations than the U.S. graduate statement convention prefers.


### 5.9 Reader Draft Prompt

Write the first paragraph of a graduate personal statement for the field you would most plausibly apply to in graduate school (or have applied to). The paragraph should: state a specific research question; name a specific prior project or experience that anchors the question; do not begin with a childhood anchor.

Save the paragraph. Compare it (in Chapter 17) to the opening line you saved at the end of Chapter 1. Notice the genre difference.


### 5.10 Exercises

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: The Graduate School Personal Statement
blocks.src:
#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What is the central reorientation between the undergraduate essay and the graduate statement?

**Answer:** The reader's question shifts from _who is this person?_ to _what research direction is this person prepared to pursue?_ Graduate readers read for evidence of a research orientation; childhood anchors and emotional vulnerability are out of place. The graduate statement is a research document with the candidate behind it, not a personal narrative with intellectual gestures.

**Q2.** Why is the statement _I am interested in cognitive neuroscience_ insufficient as a graduate research interest?

**Answer:** It is a topic, not a question. Topics are too broad to indicate readiness for graduate-level research. A question is more specific (e.g., _I want to understand whether the bilingual advantage in attentional control is robust across socioeconomic strata_). The question may turn out to be wrong or may be revised; what matters is that the candidate can articulate one.

**Q3.** What four questions should each piece of evidence in a graduate statement answer?

**Answer:** (1) What was the question being investigated? (2) What did the candidate specifically do? (3) What was the result, and what did the candidate learn (including from what did not work)? (4) How does this lead to the candidate's current research interest?

**Q4.** Why is the over-confident closing a pitfall in graduate statements?

**Answer:** Graduate committees know that two-year and six-year research predictions are rarely accurate. A candidate who claims certainty about exactly what they will work on for years signals naivety about how research evolves. The Restrained Connection from Chapter 2 applies: state plans concretely while acknowledging the specific question will evolve.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: The Graduate School Personal Statement
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1. Convert undergraduate to graduate register.**

A candidate's draft graduate statement opens:

> Ever since I was a child, I have been fascinated by the human brain. Watching my grandmother decline from Alzheimer's disease over the past decade has shaped my understanding of memory and identity in profound ways. As an undergraduate, I have pursued these interests through coursework in psychology, neuroscience, and philosophy.

Rewrite this opening in the graduate register. You may invent plausible specifics consistent with a candidate interested in memory research who has worked in a behavioral neuroscience lab and has co-authored a poster.

Hint

The childhood-anchor opening must go. Replace with a research question and a specific prior project.

**Answer:**

> The question I am applying to study is how spatial reorganization of memory traces during sleep is altered in early-stage Alzheimer's, and whether the alteration precedes overt cognitive decline. The question came into focus during my senior thesis in Professor Reinhart's lab, where I helped run a polysomnography study of 24 participants in the early-MCI stage and 24 age-matched controls. We found a 38% reduction in slow-wave sleep coherence between hippocampal and prefrontal sites in the MCI group, replicating recent work from the Stickgold lab but in a cohort of slightly earlier disease progression. The grandmother-with-Alzheimer's anchor (which is true; my grandmother was diagnosed when I was eleven) is not why I am applying to graduate school. The 38% finding, and what it does and does not yet imply, is.

The rewrite preserves the personal anchor as a brief acknowledgment in the second-to-last sentence rather than as the opening. The opening is the research question and the senior-thesis evidence. The candidate's identity remains visible without dominating the document.

**Q2. Diagnose the fit paragraph.**

> I would be honored to work with the distinguished faculty at MIT, including Professor X, Professor Y, and Professor Z, all of whom have made significant contributions to the field. I look forward to engaging with cutting-edge research and contributing to the vibrant intellectual community at MIT.

Identify the pitfalls and rewrite the paragraph using two specific faculty engagements.

Hint

The current version commits the faculty-name-drop pitfall and the brochure-echo pitfall.

**Answer:** Pitfalls: faculty-name-drop without engagement (X, Y, Z named but no specific reason); brochure echo (_distinguished faculty, significant contributions to the field, cutting-edge research, vibrant intellectual community_); inflated language (_I would be honored_); generic closing.

A rewrite (using specific made-up faculty for illustration):

> I would most want to work with Professor Tenenbaum, whose 2020 paper on probabilistic program induction frames a question I have been pursuing in my honors thesis on category learning under sparse data. The hierarchical-Bayesian framework his lab uses would give me the machinery to test the specific generalization question my behavioral data raise. I am also drawn to Professor Saxe's work on the developmental origins of theory of mind; her use of fMRI in 4- to 8-year-olds is exactly the methodological orientation I would like to learn, and the question of how Bayesian frameworks scale to younger participants is one I expect to encounter in my own work.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: The Graduate School Personal Statement
blocks.src:
The rewrite engages with two faculty members specifically, names a paper and a methodological framework for one and a developmental application for the other, and connects each to the candidate's prior work. The reader can verify that the candidate has done the engagement.


#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** The chapter argues that a personal anchor (e.g., a grandmother with Alzheimer's) belongs as a brief acknowledgment, not as the opener, in a graduate statement. Some statements successfully open with a personal scene. What makes a personal opener work in this register, when it works?

**Discussion:** A personal opener can work in a graduate statement when it is _very brief_ (one to three sentences), _specifically tied to a research question,_ and _immediately followed_ by the research question in concrete form. The opener is not narrative; it is a hook that says _here is the personal entry point to a question I will now describe in research terms._ The pattern is: scene (one sentence), connection (one sentence), research question (one to two sentences). What does not work: a paragraph of personal narrative without the research question following immediately. The reader needs to know within the first 60 seconds that the document is a research document; longer personal narratives delay this signal.

**Q2.** The chapter recommends naming exactly two to three faculty in the fit paragraph. Why not name one (showing focus) or five (showing thoroughness)?

**Discussion:** One signals over-reliance on a single advisor. Graduate-level work usually requires distributed mentorship; a candidate who has identified only one possible advisor signals they have not yet imagined the program's actual structure (multiple committee members, breadth requirements, methodological cross-pollination). Five signals lack of focus or padding. Two to three is the range that signals _I have done the work to identify specific fit and have selected the most relevant among them._ The deeper observation: the number itself is less important than the specificity of engagement with each. One faculty named with deep engagement is better than five named with shallow engagement.

**Q3.** Honest acknowledgment of uncertainty (e.g., _my research interest may shift; I do not yet know if I will pursue a PhD_) is a recommended convention in the closing. Could honesty about uncertainty be misread as lack of commitment? When does honesty cross into self-undermining?

**Discussion:** The line falls roughly here: honest acknowledgment of _intellectual_ uncertainty (the question may evolve; the methods may shift; the eventual specialization is not yet set) signals research maturity. Self-undermining acknowledgment of _commitment_ uncertainty (_I might decide graduate school isn't for me;_ _I haven't really thought about whether I'm a good fit_) signals the wrong thing. The chapter's recommended honesty is the first kind. It does not say _I might not finish._ It says _I expect the specific question to evolve; I will use the program to find out._ The committee reads the first as maturity and the second as warning.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 5: The Graduate School Personal Statement
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

The graduate personal statement is a research document with the candidate behind it, not a personal narrative with intellectual gestures. The reader is Professor Lay on a Saturday morning, looking for a research direction and evidence the candidate is prepared to pursue it.

The 6 Moves recalibrate to the graduate register: Move 2 finds a research story; Move 3's hook is the research question; Move 4's specifics are paradigms, papers, methods, and results; Move 6's AI test is harsher because graduate statements are highly vulnerable to AI generation.

The next chapter (Chapter 6) treats the PhD statement of purpose, where the genre tightens further: the same conventions plus the apprenticeship logic of doctoral admission, where committees are choosing future colleagues and the candidate must signal future-colleague fit.

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 6: The PhD Statement of Purpose
blocks.src:
Faculty in graduate-program admissions have estimated that roughly 70 percent of PhD statements of purpose sent to humanities departments are formulaic to the point of being indistinguishable. The other 30 percent get read carefully.

This is the central asymmetry of the form. The PhD statement of purpose (SOP) is, on paper, a one-document task. In practice, it is a high-stakes apprenticeship application: a committee of faculty is deciding whether to bring the candidate into a five-to-seven-year mentoring relationship that will end in a credential they will personally vouch for. The committee reads the SOP not only for evidence of preparation but for evidence that this candidate is someone they want to spend that long working with.

This chapter is about writing the document that lands in the 30 percent.


### 6.1 Vignette: Theo Drafts a PhD SOP

Theo is now in the senior year of college. After the master's-program statements from Chapter 5, Theo is also applying directly to PhD programs in cognitive science, on the advice of two undergraduate research mentors who have suggested that Theo's research record may be strong enough to skip the master's at certain programs.

Theo's first draft of the PhD SOP opens:

> I have always been fascinated by the human mind. Throughout my undergraduate career, I have pursued this fascination through coursework in cognitive science, psychology, and computer science, while also conducting hands-on research in three different laboratories.

Theo sends the draft to Professor Ramirez, the senior faculty mentor who has supervised Theo's honors thesis. Professor Ramirez returns it on a Sunday with a one-line note: _Drop the personal opener — at this level, the reader is already asking what your dissertation will be about, and you have eight minutes to tell them._

Theo, by now familiar with this kind of feedback, cuts. But Theo also misunderstands the second half of the comment until Professor Ramirez clarifies on Monday morning: _PhD committees expect the SOP to read as a polished piece of academic prose written by someone preparing to become an academic. They are not reading a first impression. They are reading a writing sample of the kind of prose this candidate will produce as a graduate student._

Theo realizes the SOP is closer to an academic article, in compressed form, than to a personal statement. The genre's rules tighten accordingly.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 6: The PhD Statement of Purpose
blocks.src:
### 6.2 What PhD Committees Actually Do

The PhD admissions committee is structurally different from the master's admissions committee at most institutions. The PhD committee at a research-intensive university typically consists of two to five faculty members in the candidate's subfield, plus the program director. The committee meets multiple times during the cycle. Each statement is read by at least two faculty before any decision; finalists are read by the full committee.

Reading time is longer than for master's statements. A PhD SOP is typically read in 10–20 minutes by the first reader, with second readers spending 5–10 minutes on a focused re-read. Faculty take notes. They sometimes flag specific sentences for committee discussion. They sometimes flag specific paragraphs as evidence of strong (or weak) writing.

Stacked on the universal pattern in §2.10, PhD faculty specifically weigh:

  1. **A research direction specific enough to suggest the next two papers.** A question is not enough. The faculty reader is asking, _can I imagine this candidate's first publication?_ If yes, the SOP is doing serious work. If no, the SOP is too vague.
  2. **Methodological depth, not just awareness.** A behavioral candidate who has run subjects, designed paradigms, and worked with messy data is differently prepared from a candidate who has read about behavioral methods. Faculty distinguish between the two within minutes.
  3. **A faculty fit built on the faculty's _recent_ work.** Not the highly cited paper from a decade ago. The current line of work. The thing the faculty member is actually thinking about right now.
  4. **A future-colleague signal.** Faculty are asking whether they want to spend five to seven years with this person. It is a combination of voice, judgment, and intellectual posture — the candidate reads as a future colleague rather than as a strong undergraduate.

The form-specific failure modes are:

  1. **An undergraduate-essay register.** Personal narrative, emotional reflection, inflated language about the field. The PhD SOP is professional prose addressed to a professional audience.
  2. **Faculty fit anchored on decade-old highly cited papers.** Signals the candidate has not engaged with the current state of the faculty member's work.
  3. **Confidence that the dissertation is already figured out.** Faculty know dissertations evolve over years; a candidate who claims certainty is either naive or padding.


### 6.3 Genre Conventions

The PhD SOP has the tightest conventions of any form in this book. Departures from convention are read as departures from preparation.


#### The Compressed-Article Structure

A successful PhD SOP reads like a compressed academic article: introduction (research direction), methods (what the candidate has done), findings (what the candidate's work has produced and what questions it has opened), fit (named faculty engaging with current work), and conclusion (specific plans plus honest acknowledgment of evolution). The proportions vary by field, but the structure is recognizable across cognitive science, English literature, history, computer science, philosophy.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 6: The PhD Statement of Purpose
blocks.src:
#### The First Paragraph Convention

The first paragraph states the research direction in concrete form _and_ anchors it to specific prior work. It is not a personal anchor. It is not a topic. It is a research direction with at least one specific paper or project mentioned by name.

A standard variant:

> The research direction I propose to pursue in graduate school is [X]. The direction emerged from [specific prior project], in which [specific finding]. The next question this raises is [Y], and answering it will require [methodological approach].

This four-sentence template is not mandatory but is widely successful. It compresses the essentials into a paragraph the reader can absorb quickly.


#### The Evidence Convention

The body of the SOP develops two to three pieces of independent evidence. Each piece should be a _project_ that the candidate owned (not a class assignment), with specific methods, results, and intellectual takeaways. The evidence is presented in research-paper register: _We collected data on N participants;_ _I implemented X using framework Y;_ _The result was Z, which suggests W and is inconsistent with V._


#### The Faculty Fit Convention (PhD Variant)

The faculty fit paragraph is more demanding for PhD applications than for master's applications. The candidate must:

* Name two to four faculty members.
* For each, engage with at least one _recent_ (within the last three to five years) paper or project.
* Connect the engagement to the candidate's own work.
* Suggest a possible collaboration or a question the candidate would pursue under that faculty's mentorship.

The depth required is roughly one full paragraph per faculty named, or three to five sentences if naming three faculty in 1,200 words.


#### The Methodological-Honesty Convention

A PhD SOP should acknowledge what the candidate does _not_ yet know how to do. Faculty respect honesty and recognize naivety in candidates who claim methodological mastery they have not earned. A two-sentence acknowledgment — _My methodological preparation includes X and Y; I have begun Z but have not yet [specific deeper task in Z]_ — signals readiness for the actual learning that will happen in graduate school.


#### The Closing Convention

The closing of a PhD SOP is concrete plans plus honest acknowledgment of evolution. _I expect to spend the first two years on [X], then transition to [Y]. The specific shape of [Y] will depend on what [X] produces; I expect the question to refine substantially during that period._ The closing should also acknowledge that the candidate has chosen this program for specific reasons, briefly stated.


### 6.4 The 6 Moves Applied


#### Move 1: The Reader

The faculty member reading on a Saturday afternoon between writing their own paper and fetching their child from soccer. The reader has read four other SOPs this morning, two of which were variants of the same vague enthusiasm and one of which was promising. The reader is looking for the next promising one.


#### Move 2: The Research Direction

Move 2 in the PhD SOP is _find the specific research direction._ The direction must be specific enough to suggest the next two papers but broad enough that the candidate's actual interests can fit within it. Too narrow (a single experiment) signals no breadth. Too broad (a topic) signals no specificity.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 6: The PhD Statement of Purpose
blocks.src:
#### Move 3: The Hook

The hook is the research direction stated concretely in the first two sentences. There is no other acceptable hook in this register. Personal anecdotes, surprising claims, scene-openings — these are tools of the undergraduate genre. The PhD SOP opens with research.


#### Move 4: Show With Specifics

The specifics in a PhD SOP are: paper titles, project descriptions, methods, results, faculty names, recent faculty papers, methodological tools, data sets, sample sizes. The Specific Object Test in this register requires academic specifics.


#### Move 5: Connect Specifics to Claims

The claim being supported is _I am ready to begin the apprenticeship of becoming a researcher in this field._ The specifics support the claim by demonstrating, not asserting, intellectual independence. The Restrained Connection in this register is academic restraint: state the work, state the result, state what it suggests, do not over-claim what it learned you.


#### Move 6: Survive the AI Test

PhD SOPs are vulnerable to AI generation in the same way master's statements are. The AI test is harsher: _would the SOP read identically if the candidate's specific paper-in-revision and specific 38% finding and specific faculty-paper-engaged-with were swapped for any other set of these things?_ If yes, the AI test fails. The remedy is concrete academic specifics.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 6: The PhD Statement of Purpose
blocks.src:
### 6.5 Theo's PhD SOP Revised

Theo, after Professor Ramirez's intervention, rewrites. The new opening:

> The research direction I propose to pursue in graduate school is the developmental trajectory of bilingual attentional control across socioeconomic contexts, with particular attention to whether the standard bilingual advantage is a robust developmental effect or partly a confound of correlated variables in the populations typically sampled. The question first surfaced for me as an undergraduate observation about the homes of the bilingual children I worked with — heritage-language exposure that varied widely along socioeconomic lines and that the standard paradigms did not capture — and reached experimental form in my honors thesis completed this past spring, in which we replicated the bilingual advantage in 78 children aged 6–9 in a high-income school district (d = 0.42) and failed to replicate it in 78 children in a low-income district (d = 0.04, n.s.). The next question this raises is whether the divergence reflects genuine moderation by socioeconomic context or methodological confounds that have been masked in prior bilingual-advantage research. Answering it will require a paradigm that controls for parental input in matched bilingual and monolingual groups across socioeconomic strata, with attentional measures sensitive to small effects (we used the child Stroop; the next paradigm should use either the Attention Network Task or a flanker task with greater statistical power).

This 195-word opening paragraph does what the genre requires: states the research direction, anchors to a specific project with results, names the next question, and sketches the methodological approach. The reader, two minutes in, has placed Theo as a candidate with a specific paper-in-progress and a defensible plan for the dissertation's first study.

Run the 6 Moves:

* **Move 1** : Done. The faculty reader places Theo within seconds.
* **Move 2** : Done. The research direction is specific and anchored.
* **Move 3** : Done. The opening sentence does the hook in research register.
* **Move 4** : Done. Specifics include the lab, the year, the sample sizes, the effect sizes, the school districts, the paradigms named.
* **Move 5** : Done. The claim _I am ready_ is implicit; the specifics demonstrate it.
* **Move 6** : Done. The d = 0.42 / d = 0.04 specific finding is not generic; an AI given a generic prompt would not produce it.

The remainder of the SOP develops two more pieces of evidence (a coursework project on cross-linguistic statistical analysis; a summer of pilot work in El Salvador), the faculty fit paragraph, the methodological honesty paragraph, and the closing.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 6: The PhD Statement of Purpose
blocks.src:
### 6.6 A Complete Sample PhD SOP

Below is a complete original sample (~1,300 words) by a fictional applicant, Daniel, applying to a PhD program in English literature.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 6: The PhD Statement of Purpose
blocks.src:
> The research direction I propose to pursue is the role of mid-twentieth-century working-class print cultures — labor union newsletters, ethnic-press serial fiction, and small-town reprint papers — in shaping post-1945 American literary realism, with particular attention to writers whose first published work appeared in these venues before reaching commercial fiction markets. The direction emerged from my senior thesis at Wesleyan, _The Reprint Geography of Hisaye Yamamoto's Early Stories_ completed in 2024, in which I tracked the publication and reprint history of seven Yamamoto stories across the _Pacific Citizen,_ the _Rafu Shimpo,_ and several less-cataloged ethnic-press serials between 1947 and 1953, before her commercial debut in the _Partisan Review._
> 
> The thesis produced two findings. First, six of the seven stories appeared in at least three ethnic-press venues before reaching the _Partisan Review_ — a circulation pattern that has been undocumented in existing Yamamoto scholarship, which has tended to treat her _Partisan Review_ publication as her literary debut. Second, the textual variants between ethnic-press and commercial-press versions are non-trivial: in two stories, scenes featuring Japanese-language dialogue were rewritten in English-paraphrased form for the commercial venues, while remaining in Japanese in the ethnic-press versions. The variants raise questions about audience-specific composition that, as far as I have been able to determine, have not been pursued in the secondary literature.
> 
> The next question this raises is whether the audience-specific composition I documented in Yamamoto's case is generalizable across the cohort of mid-century Asian-American, Black, and Jewish writers who circulated in similar ethnic-press networks before commercial publication, and whether the variants constitute a distinct form of authorial doubling that has been obscured by the post-publication critical tradition's reliance on commercial-press editions. The proposed dissertation would extend the comparative method developed in my thesis to roughly twelve to fifteen authors across three ethnic-press networks (Japanese-American, African-American, and Jewish-American), with archival work centered on the Densho Digital Repository, the Schomburg Center, and the YIVO Institute.
> 
> My research preparation comes from three sources. First, the senior thesis described above, which I expect to revise into an article-length manuscript over the next year and present at the American Studies Association graduate-student conference in November. Second, a 2023 summer fellowship at the Schomburg Center, where I worked with the _Negro Quarterly_ archive on a separate project tracking Ralph Ellison's editorial correspondence; the project did not produce publishable findings, but it gave me working knowledge of the archive's catalog system and the methodological practice of reading editorial correspondence as a form of literary evidence. Third, coursework in archival methods (LIBR 575, Wesleyan), comparative literature (CLIT 380, Reading Joyce in Translation), and a graduate-level seminar in twentieth-century American fiction (ENGL 690, the only graduate seminar I was permitted to take as an undergraduate, on Bakhtinian readings of post-1945 American novels).
> 
> The methodological orientation I bring is a comparative-archival approach informed by book-history methods (Robert Darnton, Leah Price), cultural-studies approaches to print cultures (Michael Denning's _The Cultural Front,_ which I have read three times), and ethnic-studies frameworks for thinking about audience and address (Lisa Lowe's later work has been formative). I have less preparation in the digital-humanities methods that have become central to print-culture work in the past decade. I have done basic text-comparison using DiffMatchPatch and have begun learning the relevant Python tooling for stylometry, but I have not yet completed a project that uses these methods at scale. I would expect to develop these methods substantially during the program.
> 
> Yale's English program is the program I am most committed to applying to for three specific reasons. First, Professor Wai Chee Dimock's recent work on planetary literary networks, particularly the 2022 essays on translation and circulation, frames my project's circulation-and-variants question at the right scale; her methodological example is the closest I have found to what I want to do. Second, Professor Caleb Smith's work on prison literatures and the textual production of marginalized voices speaks directly to the audience-and-address questions in my project, and his recent book on attention and reading practices would enter my project's theoretical frame. Third, Yale's relationship with the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, particularly the Beinecke's strong holdings in mid-century leftist publishing, would provide archival materials I cannot access at most other programs, and the Beinecke's recent partnership with the YIVO Institute on cataloging would be especially relevant to the Jewish-American component of my proposed dissertation.
> 
> Two acknowledgments belong in this statement. First, my dissertation question will likely refine substantially during the program. The current scope (twelve to fifteen authors, three networks) is the proposal scope, not the dissertation scope; I expect the dissertation to focus on six to eight authors and one or two networks, with the specific selection determined by archival access and what the early chapters reveal. Second, I expect to need to retool methodologically. The digital-humanities side of the project requires methods I have begun but not yet mastered; I would prioritize Yale's DH summer institutes in my first year.
> 
> What I hope to do during the program: complete a chapter-length pilot study on three Yamamoto stories during my first year, expanded into a comprehensive Asian-American case study by the end of year two; transition to comparative work across the three networks during years three and four; have at least one chapter under article submission by year four. I would also like to teach in the program's Directed Studies sequence — both because I have wanted to teach in a great-books program for years and because the experience of teaching across genres would inform the comparative method of the dissertation. I do not yet know which secondary advisor I would propose; I have included Professors Smith and Dimock as primary directions, but I would also be interested in conversation with Professor Jonathan Kramnick about reading-practices methodology, which has informed my thinking about audience and may become a methodological tool for the project.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 6: The PhD Statement of Purpose
blocks.src:
This SOP is approximately 1,300 words. It performs the genre's work:

* States the research direction with specificity in the first paragraph.
* Develops the senior thesis as the primary evidence with concrete findings (specific archival sources, specific variants, specific authors).
* Acknowledges what the secondary work did _not_ produce (the Schomburg fellowship), as honest research preparation.
* Names methodological preparation honestly, including specific tools and gaps.
* Names three faculty with engagement with their _recent_ work (Dimock 2022 essays, Smith's recent book on attention).
* Acknowledges the dissertation's likely evolution and the candidate's likely retooling.
* Closes with concrete plans plus an additional faculty engagement (Kramnick) that signals breadth.

The SOP would land in the 30 percent. Whether Daniel is admitted depends on the cohort and the program's needs that year — but the document has done its work.


#### A Note on Recommendation Letters for PhD Applications

PhD applications typically require three to five letters of recommendation, and the letters carry substantial weight — at most programs, more weight than the SOP itself. The brag sheet from §13.5 is essential preparation: a one-to-three-page document for each recommender, listing specific projects you worked on with that recommender, specific moments they might mention, and the methodological questions the application asks them to address. The brag sheet's marginal return is highest for PhD applications because the letters are the parts of the file the candidate cannot otherwise control.


### 6.7 Common Pitfalls

**Pitfall 1: The undergraduate register.** The candidate writes the PhD SOP as if it were a college essay — opening with a personal anchor, using emotional language, claiming inspiration. PhD committees register this immediately as wrong-genre.

**Pitfall 2: The decade-old paper engagement.** The candidate engages with a faculty member's most-cited paper from ten or fifteen years ago, missing the faculty member's current line of work entirely. The committee reads this as the candidate having Googled the faculty member rather than having read them.

**Pitfall 3: The dissertation-already-figured-out claim.** The candidate states with confidence the exact dissertation they will write. The committee knows this is unrealistic. The candidate has signaled naivety.

**Pitfall 4: The methodological-overclaim.** The candidate claims facility with methods they have not used. Faculty can detect this within minutes — the methods discussion lacks the texture of someone who has actually done the work. Honest acknowledgment of methodological gaps is a stronger move.

**Pitfall 5: The CV-in-prose.** The candidate translates the CV into sentences. The SOP loses its function as a complement to the CV and becomes redundant. The remedy is to discuss the _trajectory_ of the work and what it has produced intellectually, not to enumerate the work.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 6: The PhD Statement of Purpose
blocks.src:
### 6.8 Cultural and ESL Calibration
